title: Lesley-Ann L. Dupigny-Giroux | Climate Collaborative
text: Lesley-Ann L. Dupigny-Giroux Appointments Climatologist 2026 Fall Biography Dr. Dupigny-Giroux is a Professor of Climatology in the Department of Geography and Geosciences, the Vermont State Climatologist since 1997, and the President of the American Association of State Climatologists from 2020-2022. In 2020, she was appointed by the Vermont House of Representatives to the Vermont Climate Council as the member with expertise in climate change science. Dr. Dupigny-Giroux teaches introductory and intermediate-level courses in climatology, physical geography and remote sensing. Her advanced level capstone seminars delve into Climatology and Natural Hazards, as well as Satellite Climatology and Land-Surfaces Processes. Many of her courses are Service-Learning collaborations with municipalities across the state, State of Vermont Agencies, and Federal entities such as NOAA. She holds a B.Sc. in Physical Geography and Development Studies from the University of Toronto (1989), an M.Sc.(1992) in Climatology and Hydrology and a Ph.D. (1996) in Climatology and Geographic Information Systems from McGill University. An applied climatologist by training, Dr. Dupigny-Giroux's research interests intersect a number of interdisciplinary fields including hydroclimatic natural hazards and climate literacy, climate services, geospatial climate and land-surface processes, all within the context of our changing climate. She is an expert in floods, droughts and severe weather and the ways in which these affect the landscape and peoples of Vermont and the US Northeast. She has worked extensively with K-12 teachers and students, bringing the use of satellites, climatology and climate change to all levels of the pre-university curriculum. She is the lead editor of Historical Climate Variability and Impacts in North America, the first monograph to deal with the use of documentary and other ancillary records for analyzing climate variability and change in the North American context. A Fellow of the American Meteorological Society, Dr. Dupigny-Giroux is currently serving three-year terms on three committees/boards of the National Academies of Science, Engineering and Medicine, including the Board of Atmospheric Sciences and Climate. She was invited by the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Program (OSTP) to be a presenter on the "Climate Science Leading the Way" panel at the COP26 meeting in Glasgow, Scotland in 2021. She has contributed to all five National Climate Assessments, serving as the lead author for the Northeast Chapter of the 2018 Fourth National Climate Assessment of the US Global Change Research Program, and is an author on the national water chapter of the Fifth National Climate Assessment. title: Chuck Sams | Climate Collaborative
text: Chuck Sams Appointments Public Advocate for the Earth 2026 Fall Biography Chuck Sams brings more than 35 years of professional experience and has occupied many important leadership positions. Currently, he is Oregon’s Council Member on the Northwest Power and Conservation Council, serves as Oregon Tribes Scholar in Residence, and is a Senior Fellow with the Native Environmental Sovereignty Project at the University of Oregon’s Environmental and Natural Resources Law Center. He also is Director of Indigenous Programs at Yale’s Center for Environmental Justice and lectures at Yale’s Environmental School. Previously, Chuck was the 19th director of the National Park Service within the U.S. Department of the Interior. Chuck possesses a Master of Legal Studies in Indigenous Peoples Law from the University of Oklahoma School of Law. Additionally, he holds a Bachelor of Science in Business Administration with concentrations in Management, Communications, and Leadership from Concordia University. Chuck served as an Intelligence Specialist in the U.S. Navy with assignments at an Attack Squadron, Joint Intelligence Center Pacific Command, and Defense Intelligence Agency Headquarters. His areas of expertise included Soviet/Russian, Middle Eastern, and Chinese affairs, as well as anti-terrorism. Chuck is an enrolled citizen/tribal member of the Cayuse and Walla Walla tribes with the CTUIR. Chuck, Lori, and their daughter Ruby reside in Pendleton, Oregon. Their older children—Rose, Chauncey, and Clara—are leading fulfilling lives as adults. The family loves to camp, hike, bike, hunt, and fish. Chuck received Honorary Doctorates in Humane Letters from Portland State University and Whitman College; the 2025 LaGasse Medal (American Society of Landscape Architects); 2025 Lone Sailor Award (U.S. Navy Memorial); 2024 Oregon History Maker (Oregon Historical Society); and the Walter T. Cox Award (Clemson University Institute for Parks). title: Montgomery Fellows to Focus on the Environment | Climate Collaborative
text: Articles Montgomery Fellows to Focus on the Environment The fall lineup includes Indigenous experts in climate solutions and sustainability. Image From left, former National Park Service Director Chuck Sams, Vermont State Climatologist Lesley-Ann Dupigny-Giroux, and hydrologist Ryan Emanuel are Montgomery Fellows on campus this term. 9/18/2026 More Reading Four Montgomery Fellows to Focus on Artificial Intelligence Leading experts in the fields of climate science, environmental justice, and sustainable policy will be on campus this term to tackle the Montgomery Fellows Program's guiding question for fall: Climate Solutions: Wishful Thinking or Hopeful Planning? Hydrologist and author Ryan Emanuel , longtime Vermont State Climatologist Lesley-Ann Dupigny-Giroux , and former National Park Service Director Chuck Sams will share their expertise on climate adaptation and sustainability through classroom visits, public lectures, and even a paddle on the Connecticut River. During their weeks on campus, the fellows also will also meet with the House Communities , Dartmouth Climate Collaborative , Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences , Department of Native American and Indigenous Studies , and the Environmental Studies Program . "Climate change is not just a science problem—it's an everyone problem—and we need leaders across disciplines and professions to move the needle," says Meredith Kelly , the faculty director of the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative. "The Montgomery Fellows this fall exemplify the critical type of climate leadership that brings together science, environmental justice, and sustainable policy." Quote The Montgomery Fellows this fall exemplify the critical type of climate leadership that brings together science, environmental justice, and sustainable policy. Attribution Meredith Kelly, faculty director, Dartmouth Climate Collaborative Steve Swayne , director of the Montgomery Fellows Program, says he has been interested for several years in bringing fellows who are focused on climate issues to campus. "It has been a privilege of ours to partner with Meredith and others in the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative on this term," Swayne says. "And I'm thrilled beyond belief that, in fostering this partnership, we also get to deepen our ties with our colleagues who work on Indigenous issues." Melanie Taylor , chair of the Department of Native American and Indigenous Studies, says the "diverse line-up of Montgomery visitors, and their engagement with a wide range of students, faculty, staff, and researchers at Dartmouth, is a good reminder that Indigenous ecological knowledge is not exclusive or proprietary, but shared and applied widely across multiple borders." Ryan Emanuel, Sept. 21 to Oct. 2 Emanuel, a citizen of the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina who co-chairs the Community Engagement and Environmental Justice concentration at Duke University, where he is a professor of hydrology, will discuss his award-winning book, On the Swamp: Fighting for Indigenous Environmental Justice. The book focuses on eastern North Carolina, Emanuel says, but he hopes its underlying concepts regarding "what it means to engage meaningfully and ethically with Indigenous peoples" are highly transferable to the Dartmouth region as well. Emanuel's public talk is set for Sept. 30 from 4:30 to 6 p.m. The location will be posted in the coming week. While on campus, he also will attend the Artificial Intelligence and Indigenous Innovations Symposium Sept. 21 to 22, and host a paddling trip on the Connecticut River at noon on Sept. 23. Visits with faculty members and students, including Climate Scholars , are also on the docket for Emanuel, who is especially keen to talk with students and early career professionals about community-based research and explore potential collaborations with Dartmouth scholars. "When we think about what appropriate resilience and adaptation to climate change looks like, we can find answers in the longstanding practices of Indigenous communities," Emanuel says. "I'm interested in learning more about what those practices look like in your region," and exploring how strategies in North Carolina communities might translate to other places, "including New England." As for the central question, wishful thinking or hopeful planning, he is optimistic. "I think that as more people become aware of climate change through their own personal encounters with extreme weather—flooding, droughts, and so forth, more and more people will wake up," Emanuel says. "And we're more likely to try something different, once we know that the same old practices may not work for dealing with climate change." Lesley-Ann Dupigny-Giroux, Oct. 5 to 16 An award-winning scientist and the longest serving state climatologist in the nation, Dupigny-Giroux is a climatology professor at the University of Vermont and former president of the American Association of State Climatologists. Being on campus will be "a truly immersive experience," says Dupigny-Giroux , an expert in climate education at the kindergarten to undergraduate levels. "There are so many innovative and creative programs in place across Dartmouth that I have only heard about from afar," she says. "I am especially excited to visit the Dartmouth Organic Farm, experience firsthand some of the cutting-edge solutions in the sustainability and net-zero spaces, and learn more about the energy innovations being deployed on campus." Her most recent collaboration "involves walking alongside Abenaki elder and scholar Judy Dow," Dupigny-Giroux says. Their working relationship and friendship was forged on the Vermont Climate Council, where they helped co-author Climate and Climate Change in Vermont , a foundational chapter of the state's 2025 Climate Action Plan. Since then, as part of the Climate Resiliency Fellowship for K-12 teachers offered by Shelburne Farms in Vermont, they have been co-teaching, which includes their presentation, "Braiding: Learning From the Land to Adapt to a Changing Climate." Dupigny-Giroux, who counts among her passions "the sharing of knowledge and understanding of climatology," says she looks forward to chatting with postdoctoral fellows and Dartmouth students "at all career stages." "Mentoring and giving back to the community are two of my core values," says Dupigny-Giroux, who often incorporates service-learning collaborations with state and federal agencies into her courses. Dupigny-Giroux's research interests include climate literacy and hydroclimatic natural hazards, such as heatwaves, floods, and drought, and climate services—scientific information and services used to help organizations and individuals adapt to climate variability and change. She will give a public lecture on the implications of droughts across Vermont's North Country on Oct. 14 from 4:30 to 6 p.m. The location will be announced later this term. While on campus, she will also connect with colleagues in several departments and institutes "to explore synergies and new collaborations," Dupigny-Giroux says. "I am hoping that my visit is deeply symbiotic and co-creative in ways that will benefit all with whom I have the privilege of interacting." Chuck Sams, Nov. 2 to 6 Sams splits his time between Connecticut—where he directs the Indigenous programs at Yale's Center for Environmental Justice and lectures at Yale's Environmental School—and his home in Oregon, where he serves in several leadership roles. An enrolled member of the Cayuse and Walla Walla of the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation, Sams served as the director of the National Park Service from 2021 to 2025. He is the Oregon Tribes Scholar in Residence and a senior fellow with the Native Environmental Sovereignty Project at the University of Oregon's Environmental and Natural Resources Law Center. Sams wrote the strategic plan for Oregon's climate resiliency executive order and now serves on the cabinet that oversees its implementation. Like Dupigny-Giroux and Emanuel, he is looking forward to exchanging ideas about sustainability and climate mitigation strategies. That includes hearing about challenges and best management practices in the Eastern United States, information he can bring back to agencies in the West, says Sams, who represents Oregon on the Northwest Power and Conservation Council. And, he stresses the importance of Indigenous knowledge regarding climate solutions. There have been three or four major global climate events over the past 30,000 years, and each time Indigenous people in the Americas adapted, mitigated the impact, and became more resilient, Sams says. "We are only now scratching the surface" of that history, which includes forest management and other land use practices, he says. "We have an opportunity to work with Native people who still have that long memory of their stories." Sams—whose professional experience spans Native American history, federal policy and policymaking, federal Indian law, international Indigenous law, and natural resource management—also welcomes the chance to interact with students. "I'm happy to sit and visit with students about their experiences and opportunities for them as they progress through their education and figure out what they want to do with their careers," he says. "Because my career is definitely not linear." Looking ahead, he hopes to continue working with Dartmouth faculty, staff, and students. "I'm very fortunate to be asked to be a Montgomery Fellow and to begin this relationship with Dartmouth," Sams says. "If I can be of support, I want to be." Sams's public talk is set for Nov. 5 from 4:30 to 6 p.m. Later this year The winter Montgomery Fellows Program series, Like a Good Neighbor , will bring together researchers to assess what it means for Dartmouth to be a good neighbor to those who live near campus, and how it could improve. Sociologist Manuel Pastor , historian Ira Harkavy , and community medicine physician Laura Gottlieb will join local leaders and academics and students and faculty from across the four schools for the conversation. In the spring, two Mexican artists will lead an immersive exploration of making and displaying public art. Performance artist and actress Katia Tirado and artist and cultural activist Lorena Wolffer will work in partnership with the departments of Spanish and Portuguese and Studio Art and the Hood Museum of Art . Written by Aimee Minbiole Share this Aimee Minbiole can be reached at aimee.minbiole@dartmouth.edu

title: Elevating Collaboration and Innovation at Climate Week NYC | Climate Collaborative
text: Articles Elevating Collaboration and Innovation at Climate Week NYC Dartmouth's largest presence yet centers on local resilience and sustainable energy. Image 9/17/2026 More Reading Dartmouth to Host Climate Week Dartmouth's third year at Climate Week NYC will be its most robust presence yet, with events that showcase the university's strengths in leveraging collaboration and innovation, both locally and internationally, to address the climate crisis. This year's events , which begin Sept. 22, are coordinated by the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative in partnership with the Sustainability Office , the Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy and Society , and the Institute of Arctic Studies . The Dartmouth lineup includes: a hands-on workshop for those at the frontlines of local climate resilience; five expert panels focused on global and community-level transitions to sustainable energy; and an international dialogue on confronting the environmental and geopolitical threats facing the Arctic in ways that build on the knowledge of Indigenous peoples and safeguard their ways of life. Dartmouth undergraduates also will take part in Climate Week NYC for the first time via an exposition of student and faculty research conducted through the Energy Justice Clinic and the Dartmouth as Living Lab initiative. Meredith Kelly , a professor of Earth and planetary sciences and faculty director for the Climate Collaborative, says the events exemplify Dartmouth's specialty in bringing people from numerous sectors together to facilitate community-based responses to climate change and the global transition to sustainable energy. "Climate change is an 'everyone' problem, meaning we need all hands on deck to change the trajectory and design and implement systems that are the basis for a resilient, sustainable, and equitable future," says Kelly, who organized the events with Rosi Kerr '97 , director of the Climate Collaborative and the Sustainability Office. Quote Dartmouth is exceptionally well-positioned to lead in this space because of its expertise in climate and policy—particularly in cold and rural regions—as well as in energy systems. Attribution Meredith Kelly, Dartmouth Climate Collaborative Faculty Director "Dartmouth is exceptionally well-positioned to lead in this space because of its expertise in climate and policy—particularly in cold and rural regions—as well as in energy systems," Kelly says. "We stand out as a leader in innovating and convening the multiple stakeholders in these areas." Resilient Communities Via Local Action The events begin at noon on Sept. 22 with Resilience Action Lab: Building an Integrated Just Transition for Our Communities , an in-person "train-the-trainers" workshop ( register here to attend) for around 60 people from government agencies and nonprofit groups across New York state and the New York City area. The workshop is followed at 3 p.m. by Affordable and Resilient: Community-Based Sustainable Energy Transitions , an expert panel on how to work with local residents to realize new energy projects that benefit everyone. ( Register to attend online). The Resilience Action Lab, led by Christa Daniels , the Climate Collaborative's assistant director for community partnerships, will leverage Dartmouth research and scholarship to help attendees develop practical, equitable climate-resilience strategies that are unique to the environmental, energy, and economic realities of their communities. "Our hope is that the workshop equips local leaders to address the multiple challenges affecting local resilience like flooding, poverty, a need for increased renewable energy, and a lack of affordable and accessible housing," says Sarah Kelly , cofounder and head of Dartmouth's Energy Justice Clinic and a lecturer in geography, who will co-facilitate Daniels' workshop with Meredith Kelly. Insights from the workshop also can be integrated into Dartmouth's work helping communities in Vermont and New Hampshire develop their own climate solutions, Sarah Kelly says. She and Daniels hosted a pilot version of the workshop in Hanover Aug. 17 as part of a longer process of building climate-resilience coalitions in New England and New York. "Given an uncertain federal policy landscape, we need innovative regional and local approaches more than ever," Sarah Kelly says. "Ideally, universities can provide space and tools to explore what these solutions look like. We believe in convening coalitions of people and groups that can work together to remedy multiple problems at the same time." Barbara Will , vice provost for academic and international affairs, says that the workshop builds on the biennial Local Solutions conference Dartmouth hosted ahead of Climate Week last year for stakeholders across the Northeast—and will inform the next Local Solutions conference in 2027, which Dartmouth will host. Christa Daniels from the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative, pictured with Professor of Earth and Planetary Sciences Erich Osterberg, will lead a workshop on local climate resilience. (Photo By Beam Lertbunnaphongs '25) "Dartmouth has recognized the role we can and should play in bringing our academic strengths in climate change science and critical analysis to local communities. We are at once deeply invested in developing resilience in our local community where we live and work—the Upper Valley—and in helping other local communities across the country learn from our efforts," Will says. "Climate Week is the perfect place to showcase on a global stage the insights we've learned from working with local community partners," she says. Sarah Kelly will moderate the panel, which explores how municipalities, organizations, and communities are cooperating to design and implement energy systems that improve resilience, affordability, and sustainability on local terms. "I hope attendees walk away with new tools, insights, and inspiration for how we can accelerate a just transition to a low-carbon future in a way that builds community wealth, well-being, and engagement," Sarah Kelly says. Insights From the Arctic At 2 p.m. on Sept. 23, the Institute of Arctic Studies is partnering with the University of the Arctic and the Consulate General of Finland to host Circular Innovation and Resilient Futures: Insights from the Arctic . Now in its third year , the invitation-only event will examine how Indigenous knowledge systems, circular economy principles, sustainable resource management, and community leadership are creating practical climate solutions that can strengthen communities worldwide. This year also will include a keynote address by Tarja Halonen, who served as president of Finland from 2000 to 2012. "The Arctic is too often portrayed as a region in crisis or a new frontier for geopolitical and economic competition. But the people who live and work there have long adapted to change," says IAS director Melody Brown Burkins , Guarini '95, '98, who will moderate the discussion. "They are leaders and innovators who—if we listen—can help show us how to build a more resilient, sustainable future for the Arctic and our planet." Charlie Donovan , a clinical professor at the Tuck School of Business who will teach the upcoming course Governance and Sustainable Investment in the Arctic with Burkins, will serve as a panelist. The past year has thrust the Arctic into the news as the world's superpowers jockey over Greenland and the rapidly changing Arctic's resources and strategic position. That's likely to continue as climate change makes the Arctic both more accessible and more vulnerable. "It is a flashpoint in a lot of current political discussions and a new point of interest for business and government. It has a ton of resources that some people want to exploit. It is also experiencing global warming exponentially faster than the rest of the planet," says Will, who will give opening remarks. "For all these reasons it is a region worth thinking about, knowing about, and listening to," she says. The discussion, Will says, builds on Dartmouth's legacy of research and scholarship in the Arctic through IAS, the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences , the Thayer School of Engineering , and the Stefansson Collection on Polar Exploration . "Dartmouth is unique because of our long history of engagement with the Arctic—and because of our recognition that this engagement must always be both scientific and respectful and attentive to the perspectives and knowledge of people who live in those spaces," Will says. "Our reputation in the Arctic region is very strong and—if the last two years are any indication—people will show up to hear what we have to say," she says. Pressure Points of the Energy Transition The Irving Institute will host two in-person double events starting at 2:30 p.m. on Sept. 23 and 24 that bring together people making the decisions driving the development of emerging energy systems to discuss the sector's opportunities and challenges. "Rather than treating the energy transition as a single storyline, we've broken it into its actual pressure points: intelligent grid operations, supply-chain resilience, capital formation, and transmission financing," says Geoffrey Parker , Irving's faculty director and a panelist in both events. "These are also the exact pressure points that industry and policymakers are wrestling with today, as artificial intelligence, electrification, and reshoring accelerate demand—colliding with a grid and supply chain built for a different era," Parker says. "We hope to provide a clearer picture of where the energy transition is succeeding, where it's stalled, and what it will take to move it forward." The first event will consist of panels on intelligent, resilient power systems and on critical minerals and the energy supply chain. The event's second panel includes Irving's Distinguished Industry Fellows Giulia Siccardo '12 and, as moderator, Miranda Ballentine . "The two panels together tell a coherent story," Parker says. "Digital innovation and physical supply chains are two sides of the same coin, and neither decarbonization nor energy abundance happens without both." The second event includes a discussion on the role of capital investment in the energy transition moderated by Donovan and one about the current financing bottlenecks facing the U.S. power grid, moderated by Abigail Ross Hopper '93 , a Distinguished Industry Fellow in the Irving Institute. "The throughline is capital discipline. Investment without transmission is stranded; transmission without disciplined capital allocation is unaffordable," Parker says. "Collectively, these four panels position Dartmouth not just as a commentator on the energy transition, but as an active participant—bringing the right people into the room, spurring new research ideas, and contributing to durable solutions," he says. Showcasing Research and Making Connections At 4:15 p.m. on Sept. 22, the Climate Collaborative and Sustainability Office will host a reception for students and faculty to present and discuss their research conducted on campus and abroad. Afterward, the Dartmouth Climate Alliance will host a meet-up for alumni and students to connect and share ideas with campus climate leaders in town for the week. Leonela Espinoza Campomanes '27 will talk at Climate Week NYC about her work with renewable energy in remote locations, such as in her native Peru. (Photos courtesy of Leonela Espinoza Campomanes '27) Leonela Espinoza Campomanes '27 is one of several students who will be attending Climate Week NYC through Dartmouth. She will talk about her work on the Energy Justice Clinic project assessing the feasibility of solar energy in an Indigenous community in Chile, particularly in the cold winter months. Espinoza Campomanes, who is from Peru's capital, Lima, grew up aware of how environmental and energy challenges depend on where you live. She'd travel 1-2 hours a day to find reliable power, internet, and other basic infrastructure. Her family in her parents' native Andes Mountains lived with even less access, if they had any at all, Espinoza Campomanes says. "This is the main reason why I became interested in renewable energy. Not only the technology itself, but also the process of working with communities and making sure that projects respond to what people actually need and value," says Espinoza Campomanes, who also interned on a wind-energy project in Peru through Dartmouth. "For that reason, I am also really excited about the project in Chile because if it works great, it would be something I would love to implement in my parents' Indigenous villages, too," she says. "I consider this work a way to uplift the voice of people who are usually unheard." Espinoza Campomanes sees Climate Week NYC as an opportunity to get feedback from climate and energy experts that will advance the Chile project and her own work in off-grid energy systems, as well as expand her interest in climate science and cities. "This is an incredible opportunity to connect with other passionate people, as well as share my experiences and think about how all the work I have done and my education at Dartmouth can be part of my contribution to climate solutions," she says. text: The Irving Institute at Climate Week NYC Working alongside the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative, the Irving Institute helped drive Dartmouth's largest-ever Climate Week NYC presence this September, with seven events across the week attracting more than 800 registrants. Engagement Additional navigation Close Engagement and Collaboration Climate Week NYC Energy Ventures Alumni Four Panels, One Energy Transition “Together, our four panels on September 23 and 24 mapped the full value chain of the energy transition and explored the actual pressure points: intelligent grid operations, supply-chain resilience, capital formation, and transmission. Each panel convened the people building these systems, financing them, and regulating them—alongside Dartmouth faculty, Distinguished Industry Fellows, and alumni working across the energy landscape.” — Professor Geoffrey Parker, Faculty Director, Irving Institute for Energy and Society The Intelligent Grid: Challenges and Opportunities in an Era of AI and Electrification On Sept. 23, a panel on AI and grid intelligence, co-hosted with SAP, examined how to make smarter use of the data and assets already on the grid. Read more Read more Critical Minerals: The Supply Chain Behind the Energy Transition A Sept. 23 companion panel on critical minerals confronted the physical inputs, manufacturing, processing, and recycling capacity the energy transition requires. Read more Read more Bubble or Breakthrough: How Capital Shapes the Energy Transition On Sept. 24, a panel explored how bubbles and breakthroughs are connected and how speculative capital has repeatedly driven down the costs of new technologies. Read more Read more Beyond the Bottleneck: Financing the Grid America Needs Now On Sept. 24, a second panel examined why transmission—despite being both investable and necessary—remains stuck—and how to get it moving. title: Dartmouth Launches Climate Futures Initiative | Dartmouth
text: More news Articles Dartmouth Launches Climate Futures Initiative News subtitle Faculty are invited to three colloquia on climate scholarship and teaching. Image Image (Photo by Robert Gill) 4/16/2024 More Reading Greenshot Teams Hard at Work on Planet-Saving Startups Body How can and should Dartmouth’s institutional resources—from the forests of the Second College Grant to the Organic Farm and the central campus itself—be harnessed as laboratories for experiential learning and nationally distinctive research programs about climate change? That is the central question of the Climate Futures Initiative , a year-long effort to identify Dartmouth’s strengths and opportunities for climate scholarship and education locally, regionally, nationally, and internationally. The initiative is being led by Professor of Anthropology Laura Ogden , who was recently appointed special advisor to the provost on climate and sustainability . CFI is one of several key pillars of Dartmouth’s commitment to meaningful action to address climate change and sustainability—a priority that President Sian Leah Beilock outlined in her Inaugural address in September, pledging an aggressive push for the campus to achieve real carbon zero and to become a world leader in developing innovative, sustainable, and human-centered cold-weather climate solutions. “The goal of the Climate Futures Initiative is to capitalize on Dartmouth’s extraordinary community of scholars and students and our unique sense of place in rural New Hampshire to maximize our academic impact on climate-related issues,” says Provost David Kotz ’86 . Throughout the spring and fall, Dartmouth faculty are invited to participate in a series of three CFI colloquia to explore how the campus can become a lab for climate study and innovation. Complementary colloquia can begin to form around interdisciplinary faculty research initiatives to leverage competitive extramural research funding in support of national and international initiatives. The sessions are intended to encourage open and expansive faculty participation in the conversation around climate change, with a goal of understanding what other professors are doing in this space, coming up with actionable ideas for future research and teaching engagements, and creating community. “While pursuing multiple academic initiatives, we want the concept of ‘campus as lab’ to become one model that encourages integrative and creative thinking spanning the humanities, arts, sciences, and applied fields. In addition, we want to look well beyond the campus to train scholars for a world facing the challenges of a changing climate,” Ogden says. The first three faculty colloquia to explore the “campus as lab” model include: Campus Decarbonization and Geothermal Energy Transitions, chaired by Meredith Kelly , professor of earth sciences. Noon to 3:30 p.m., May 1. Dartmouth’s Organic Farm, chaired by Theresa Ong , assistant professor of environmental studies. Noon to 3:30 p.m., May 3. The Second College Grant, chaired by Matt Ayres , professor of biological sciences. Sept. 13 (time TBA). To register for the colloquia, faculty should email Laura.A.Ogden@Dartmouth.edu . Ogden says plans for other CFI programs are in the works on topics that include faculty pilot projects, Arctic and northern climates research, campus-wide curriculum efforts on climate change, student engagement, and strengthening Dartmouth’s global visibility in climate research. title: Dartmouth's Climate Commitment on Earth Day | Office of the President
text: Articles Dartmouth’s Climate Commitment on Earth Day 4/22/2024 Dear members of the Dartmouth community, Today, I am proud to announce the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative —a comprehensive approach that integrates our academic enterprise, campus operations, and community engagement to address climate change in meaningful and sustainable ways. First, over the next five years, Dartmouth will invest more than half a billion dollars in improvements to our physical plant to reduce emissions on campus 60% by 2030, and 100% by 2050—the largest investment focused on sustainability in our history. ( Watch the video. ) Our aging infrastructure—some of which is more than 100 years old—is in dire need of repair, and rather than sinking resources into an outdated system, we will take this opportunity to reduce our carbon footprint in a lasting way. This will include upgrades to improve energy efficiency, continuing the transition from steam to hot water heating, and the installation of geo-exchange borefields and high-capacity heat pumps in order to aggressively reduce our greenhouse gas impact. We acknowledge that our past efforts around campus decarbonization have come up short. Our new, much more aggressive goals are designed to help us lead in campus sustainability—especially in more rural cold-climate locations. Second, as a leading research university, our responsibility to address climate change goes far beyond the carbon footprint on campus. We are home to incredibly talented and accomplished scholars who have devoted their lives to studying and teaching the effects of a changing climate and developing innovative solutions to sustain our planet. We must support the vision and work of our faculty. To this end, anthropology professor Laura Ogden , who is serving as a special advisor to the provost on climate and sustainability, is leading the Climate Futures Initiative . This year-long effort, launched last week, will help ensure we capitalize on areas where Dartmouth is best positioned to drive climate scholarship and solutions—focusing on our unique sense of place, our history and ties to Native and Indigenous communities, our rural, cold-climate location, and more. Across the arts, humanities, sciences, and applied fields, we are already driving critical work: Jami Powell is curating Indigenous art at the Hood made from ash trees that are disappearing because of climate change; Professor Justin Mankin's work on climate variability is improving our understanding of human activity that has influenced snow loss in the Northern Hemisphere; The Indigenizing Arctic Research Project , a five-institution collaborative led by the Dickey Center's Institute of Arctic Studies, is informing the future of Arctic research through innovative, Indigenous-led engagement. Engineering professor Mary Albert, Thayer '83 , and her team have won international recognition for their work on an energy transition model with the people of Qaanaaq, an Arctic community in northern Greenland; And the Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy and Society and the Magnuson Center for Entrepreneurship, in partnership with the Tuck School of Business and Thayer School of Engineering, have launched the Greenshot Accelerator for climate entrepreneurs. As we embark on the largest operational change in Dartmouth's history, our campus will become a living lab as our capital projects become drivers of new research, teaching, and collaboration. Critical to this will be our students, whose passion and creativity have helped spur our aggressive push around campus decarbonization. The Dartmouth Climate Collaborative will be data driven, bring diverse perspectives to the table, and coordinate with an advisory council composed of faculty, students, alums, and a member of the community group Sustainable Hanover. The council will be led by Professor Ogden and Rosi Kerr '97 , director of the Sustainability Office. As the effects of climate change become more and more pronounced, Dartmouth must meet the moment. Maintaining the status quo is not an option, nor is incremental change. The time for bold action is now. Dartmouth has a responsibility to live up to the Big Green: a name that captures our pride in and commitment to the beautiful, natural place we live in. Sincerely, Sian Leah Beilock President Written by Office of the President Share this Tags Announcements Community Messages

title: ABOUT | Dartmouth Sustainability
text: OUR MISSION MISSION At Dartmouth Sustainability, our mission is to challenge and empower Dartmouth College and our students to take on the human and environmental problems of a rapidly changing planet. We do this via applied learning, building community, supporting teaching and scholarship, and transforming campus operations. Photo by Chris Johnson VISION We imagine a Dartmouth where: ​ Sustainability is central to how the institution operates, teaches, and does research. ​ Students see how sustainability connects to what they care about, and graduate ready to lead. ​ Anyone drawn to this work feels welcome, valued, and equipped to contribute on campus and in the Upper Valley. ​ ​ ​ ​ Dartmouth sends scholarship, solutions, and people into the world that help it flourish. HOW WE WORK Curious. We question norms, seek out many perspectives, and never stop learning. ​​ Collaborative. Complex problems need interdisciplinary teams of students, faculty, staff, community partners, and peer institutions. ​​ Inclusive. Everyone should be able to participate fully. We don't tolerate hate. ​​ Reflective. We pause, ask for feedback, and act on it. ​​ Rooted here. We care about Dartmouth and the Upper Valley, and we bring out the best of this place. ​​ Joyful. We prioritize well-being, genuine connection, and a sense of adventure. Photo by Chris Johnson WHAT WE MEAN BY "SUSTAINABILITY" Reducing Dartmouth's negative impacts and growing its positive ones. Sustainability is about balance—with natural systems, with other people, and in our own lives. It is rooted in place, shaped by culture and landscape, and demands long-term thinking that counts full cost, not just first cost. WHAT WE DO Shaping climate citizens through experiential learning that takes students out of the classroom and into the field ​ ​ Advancing scholarly excellence through grants, collaboration, and access to Dartmouth's lands and data ​ ​ Using Dartmouth's campus and lands as a living lab for climate research ​ ​ Leading on sustainable operations with projects that change how Dartmouth runs ​ ​ Partnering across the community to deliver solutions that work ​ ​ Telling the story of climate research so people are moved to act ​ Photo by Forrest Town '18 DARTMOUTH CLIMATE COLLABORATIVE The Climate Collaborative fosters connection and builds a network of strong relationships across campus. We work with faculty, staff, and students across all Dartmouth schools, including: Arts and Sciences , Geisel School of Medicine , Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies , Thayer School of Engineering , and Tuck School of Business . The Dartmouth Sustainability Office energizes the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative, providing the staffing, facilitation, and coordination that keep campus-wide climate initiatives moving forward. The Sustainability Office cultivates partnerships, develops experiential learning, and advances environmental responsibility transforming the Collaborative's vision into meaningful climate action and long-term resilience. Learn More INCLUSIVITY Sustainability problems are systemic, so solving them requires diverse perspectives and solutions that are just, equitable, and available to all. We maintain a living plan with goals and actions for centering justice, equity, diversity, and inclusion in our work. We know that work is never done. Tell us how we can do better: Office Hours, Wednesdays 12–1:30 p.m. in Robinson 106, or email us . title: Dartmouth’s Life Sciences Center Wins Platinum Award for Green Building Practices | Dartmouth
text: More news Articles Dartmouth’s Life Sciences Center Wins Platinum Award for Green Building Practices 3/26/2012 Body Dartmouth’s new Class of 1978 Life Sciences Center has just been awarded a Platinum LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) certification, the U.S. Green Building Council ’s (USGBC) highest level of recognition for energy efficient and sustainable building practices. Image The Class of 1978 Life Science Center was constructed with a high-performance building envelope incorporating high insulation values, a continuous air and vapor barrier, and solar gain control systems. (photo by Joseph Blumberg) “We are honored to receive the LEED recognition. Sustainability is a core value that we bring to all of our work in capital projects and operations,” says Linda Snyder, vice president for Campus Planning and Facilities. “It is deeply gratifying to know that the Life Sciences Center is providing a platform for our academic programs in the environmental and life sciences.” LEED is an internationally recognized mark of excellence that provides “a framework for identifying and implementing practical and measurable green building design, construction, operations and maintenance solutions,” according to the USGBC. “This is a great accomplishment for Dartmouth and the design team,” says Professor Thomas Jack , chair of the Department of Biological Sciences , which is housed in the new building. Jack was a key member of the planning team, bringing his scientific research and teaching experience to bear in the planning process. “Environmental concerns were a priority from the start, even as we interviewed architectural firms and mechanical engineers. People have been working toward this since day one, so it is pretty satisfying to see it happen.” The 174,500-square-foot Class of 1978 Life Sciences Center (LSC) has been up and running for academic business since fall term classes began in September 2011. Image The mechanics room of the Class of 1978 Life Science Center is home to many of the working parts that support and maintain the building’s sustainable practices. Operation of the LSC is showing an annual cost savings of 30 to 35 percent compared to buildings of standard construction. (photo by John Sherman) Big Green Dartmouth currently has five buildings recognized with Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) certification. They are: Class of 1978 Life Sciences Center (certified LEED platinum) McLaughlin Residential Cluster (certified LEED gold) The Fahey/McLane Residence Hall (certified LEED gold) Kemeny Hall and Haldeman Center (certified LEED silver) Floren Varsity House (certified LEED silver) Among its environmental features is an air sampling system that monitors the air continually, allowing minute adjustments in airflow that result in energy cost savings. A high-performance building envelope system with high insulation values, a continuous air and vapor barrier, and solar gain control systems minimize energy losses. Rooftop rainwater is channeled into six 10,000-gallon storage tanks and used in the building’s graywater systems, conserving drinking water for its intended use.  The water collection and treatment system minimizes runoff, reducing downstream discharge and minimizing contamination of the waterways. Several “green” roofs constructed of layered soil topped with cultivated grasses also help the energy budget. With its innovative design and imaginative execution, operation of the LSC is showing an annual energy cost savings of 30 to 35 percent when compared with buildings of standard construction. A substantial gift from the Class of 1978 made the construction of the award-winning building possible. Written by Joseph Blumberg Share this Facebook X Email Categories Campus Science & Health Tags Alumni Awards Department of Biological Sciences Ecology, Evolution, Ecosystems, and Society Graduate Program Faculty Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies Office of Sustainability Quoted Quote Everybody’s very excited about this technology and wants to see it scale up, to see the full benefits. text: Master of Energy Transition Degree Dartmouth's nine-month, residential Master of Energy Transition degree program equips early-career professionals with the interdisciplinary training, real-world experience, and expert mentorship needed to help power a more sustainable, climate-stable future. Accelerate Your Impact on Clean Energy Systems The Master of Energy Transition (MET) is a non-thesis, interdisciplinary program that equips you to lead in a rapidly evolving energy landscape. The MET takes a systems-level approach: from infrastructure and technology to economics, policy, and social equity, you'll engage with the full complexity of clean energy systems. We welcome students from all academic backgrounds. Whether you have focused on STEM, social sciences, or the humanities, there is demand for your skills and perspective in the energy transition. Studying with renowned Dartmouth faculty and supported by an industry mentor, you'll build the skills and knowledge to collaborate with stakeholders across sectors, locally and globally. Request more information Request more information Chat with our admissions manager Chat with our admissions manager Master of Energy Transition: At a Glance Program duration 9 months: September through June Delivery method In person on the Dartmouth campus Required credits 9 courses for a total of 27 credits Education Additional navigation Close Teaching and Learning at the Irving Institute Undergraduate Students Graduate Students Master of Energy Transition Degree Courses & Curriculum MET Faculty Mentorship, Networking & Community Career Treks Alumni & Careers Class of 2026 Profiles Class of 2027 Profiles Info Sessions & Admissions Events Apply to the MET Frequently Asked Questions Energy Justice Clinic Resources Join our Next Info Session After you attend an Info Session, your MET application fee will be waived! Join our faculty director, program director, and members of the MET team to hear about courses and faculty, personalized mentorship, and career treks. We'll cover the application process and close with a live Q&A. On Campus: Tuesday, October 27, 12:15 - 1:15 pm Open to the Dartmouth community | Free lunch Held at the Irving Institute for Energy and Society: The Call to Lead Lab (First floor, IR-155) Register for the on-campus Info Session Online: Tuesday, November 10, 10 - 11 am ET Open to all! Register for the online Info Session Program Highlights Earn your degree in 9 months: Complete three academic terms, beginning in September and finishing in June. Connect with a close-knit, diverse cohort: Build a lifelong network of peers and learn alongside fellow students from a wide range of disciplines and sectors. Join a dynamic community: Study on the Dartmouth campus, with abundant opportunities for co-curricular engagement, networking, and events. Receive dual support: Benefit from the full resources of the Irving Institute for Energy and Society and the Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies. Develop a broad foundation: Prepare to work across sectors through our interdisciplinary curriculum , designed to help you accelerate the development and deployment of clean, affordable, and equitable energy solutions. Chart your path through one-on-one career mentorship: Gain valuable guidance and connections from a Dartmouth alum working at the forefront of energy. "The worlds of energy and technology have converged in spectacular fashion, creating one of the defining challenges of our generation — how do we power an increasingly digital economy while keeping energy affordable, reliable, and sustainable for everyone? There has never been a more important time to develop that expertise." — Geoff Parker, Faculty Director, Irving Institute for Energy and Society Careers & Outcomes As the world shifts toward low and no-carbon energy systems, the demand for skilled professionals in energy career paths continues to increase. In 2025, global renewable energy capacity grew by more than 15.5% ( International Renewable Energy Agency ). Businesses, non-profit organizations, and government agencies need professionals who can move fluidly across sectors—from technology and finance to policy and community impact. The MET takes a systems-level approach and incorporates each of these disciplines into one comprehensive program. Alumni have gone on to roles in consulting, finance, analysis, and climate risk modeling at organizations ranging from major regional transmission organizations to leading energy consulting firms. Explore Alumni & Careers Explore Alumni & Careers Tailored Mentorship A distinctive feature of the MET program is one-on-one mentorship from Dartmouth's vast network of alumni and energy leaders. You'll be paired with a mentor whose career path aligns with your goals and interests, offering guidance and support as you build your professional identity and chart your path forward. Explore mentorship Explore mentorship Immersive Career Treks Career treks connect you with the people who are actively shaping the energy transition across technology, policy, finance, and community impact. MET students travel to major U.S. energy hubs to tour facilities, meet with staff, and get a firsthand look at where the industry stands—and where it's going. Explore Career Treks Explore Career Treks “The Institute’s mission of bringing together diverse perspectives across disciplines, sectors, and communities made this experience especially unique. Through the MET program, I had the opportunity to learn from faculty, industry leaders, policymakers, and practitioners working at the forefront of energy and climate challenges.” Rebecca Middlen GR'26, JD student, Vermont Law and Graduate School Application Information The Master of Energy Transition (MET) is part of Dartmouth's Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies . title: A Successful Launch: Dartmouth’s Inaugural Master of Energy Transition Cohort | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Articles A Successful Launch: Dartmouth’s Inaugural Master of Energy Transition Cohort Image Dartmouth's inaugural Master of Energy Transition cohort, the Class of 2026. | Photo by Beam Lertbunnaphongs '25. 9/1/2026 Within two months of graduation, 68 percent of the inaugural Master of Energy Transition cohort secured job offers or advanced study placements. Dartmouth's Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy and Society marked a major milestone in June 2026: the graduation of the inaugural class of its Master of Energy Transition (MET) program. Approved in September 2024, the MET program welcomed its first cohort of 20 students just one year later, in September 2025. From day one, this interdisciplinary program set out to do something different, pairing a systems-level approach to energy issues with tailored one-on-one mentorship and immersive career treks to industry hubs. The program's mentorship model draws deeply on Dartmouth's distinctive alumni culture. "Dartmouth is known for having one of the largest and most interconnected alumni networks. We were able to really tap into that," said Rebecca Foulkes GR'26, a member of the inaugural class now working at Halcyon, an AI platform for energy. "There are Dartmouth alumni on the Irving board, and a lot of alumni have gone into energy. That's been an incredible value-add. People come to campus and give talks. We were able to go to alumni events in New York, Boston, Houston, and San Francisco. Building that network has been incredibly valuable." Students echoed that sentiment when describing the program's signature career treks. "These visits provided invaluable opportunities to engage directly with industry leaders and practitioners across the energy and climate sectors, bridging academic learning with real-world application," said Fred Burondwa GR'26, another member of the inaugural cohort. Of the 20 students who enrolled, 19 graduated in June 2026. (One student was unable to return to the U.S. due to visa complications and hopes to complete the degree in a future year.) By July, 68 percent of graduates had already secured job offers or gained admission to doctoral and law programs. New graduates went on to organizations including BP, ENGIE, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), Grid United, Halcyon, Irving Oil, the New York Independent System Operator (NYISO), and Rhizome Data, as well as firms led by fellow Dartmouth alumni, such as Energy and Environmental Economics (E3) and the NorthBridge Group. Among them is Riley Roach GR'26, who joined Grid United, a Houston-based developer of next-generation transmission infrastructure, as a commercial analyst. "Receiving this job offer was one of the greatest 'yeses' of my life," Roach said, "second only to my acceptance into the MET program." The program's early success hasn't gone unnoticed. Members of the Irving Institute's Advisory Board and staff report growing interest from peer institutions watching closely as Dartmouth pioneers a new interdisciplinary model for graduate energy education. The intensive, cohort-based MET experience equips students with the knowledge, networks, and confidence to participate in the global energy transition. As the Class of 2026 heads off to new roles—from Houston to Washington, D.C.—the Irving Institute is delighted to welcome the next MET cohort and continue building on this strong foundation. Photo by Beam Lertbunnaphongs '25. Written by Cate Homicki Share this Tags Graduate article The Irving Institute Celebrates Inaugural MET Graduates 6/22/2026 The Irving Institute marked a milestone on June 12th with its Inaugural Graduation Celebration, honoring the MET Class of 2026.

title: Bubble or Breakthrough: How Capital Shapes the Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Articles Bubble or Breakthrough: How Capital Shapes the Energy Transition Image (From left) Andrew Beebe '93, Managing Director at Obvious Ventures; Giulia Siccardo '12, Managing Director and Head of North America at Quinbrook and Distinguished Industry Fellow at the Irving Institute; Geoff Parker, faculty director of the Irving Institute and the Charles E. Hutchinson '68A Professor of Engineering Innovation at Dartmouth; and Charlie Donovan, Professor at the Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth. (Photo By Naomi Wade) 10/2/2026 Technological innovation has always required capital, whether from speculative investors, government programs, or some combination of both. The path from promising idea to transformative technology is rarely a straight line of exponential growth. Solar, wind, and batteries all endured cycles of speculative exuberance and collapse. Federal subsidies propped up some of these technologies at critical moments; others, lacking the bridge funding needed to reach economies of scale, fell into the abyss. Now a new cohort of technologies—enhanced geothermal, fusion, small modular reactors—is running the same gauntlet, backed by capital that may prove prescient, misguided, or somewhere in between. The unsettling truth, according to a panel of investors, engineers, and scholars convened recently, is that it's almost impossible to tell the difference from inside the hype, and that hype itself can drive real breakthroughs. The discussion was held under the Chatham House Rule, so comments below are not attributed to individual speakers. A Panel of Experts The discussion was moderated by Charlie Donovan , Professor at the Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth. He was joined by Geoff Parker , faculty director of the Irving Institute and the Charles E. Hutchinson '68A Professor of Engineering Innovation at Dartmouth; Andrew Beebe '93 , Managing Director at Obvious Ventures; and Giulia Siccardo '12 , Managing Director and Head of North America at Quinbrook and Distinguished Industry Fellow at the Irving Institute. Their collective experience spans the entire capital stack, from seed-stage climate startups to multi-billion-dollar infrastructure funds. The Both/And Problem The panelists rejected the premise embedded in the panel's own title. It is not bubble or breakthrough—rather, bubbles and breakthroughs are often inextricably linked. One panelist recalled standing on the roof of Solyndra the day before the solar manufacturer declared bankruptcy, one of many casualties of the billions poured into "Clean Tech 1.0." Solar costs have since fallen 90 percent, making it the cheapest energy source in many markets today. Both the wreckage and the win arose from the same wave of capital. This is not a new pattern. One panelist offered a tour of history's speculative bubbles—canals in the 1700s, the dot-com crash, the mortgage crisis, the overbuilding of merchant power plants in the early 2000s—asserting that speculative capital has driven nearly every major technological leap. Rational, risk-adjusted capital alone, the reasoning goes, would rarely fund something as improbable as scaling an unproven technology from lab to grid. It often takes a large measure of investor exuberance to get there. (From left) Panelists Andrew Beebe '93, Giulia Siccardo '12, Geoff Parker, and moderator Charlie Donovan. | Photo by Naomi Wade. Matching Capital to Risk Where the panel found more nuance was in distinguishing types of capital and the risks for which they are suited. Venture capital, one investor explained, carries the expectation that 90 to 95 percent of bets fail—and that's true across all of venture capital, not just climate tech. The category isn't broken; simply stated, early-stage technology is always this hard. He expressed some skepticism toward venture-timelines for direct air capture, fusion, and quantum computing because they may not work on a timescale compatible with fund life cycles. Infrastructure capital operates under an entirely different logic, focused on scalability and bankability rather than technology risk. The trouble, the panelists agreed, is the "missing middle"—the gap between money for early pilots and money that flows once a technology is proven in the market. Government has historically stepped in to bridge what is also known as the "valley of death" between proof of concept and scale, but the gap remains vast and persistent. Increasingly, hyperscale tech companies are filling that role, investing at  a governmental level to ensure the technologies they need can scale. One panelist pointed to Fervo Energy's recent deal with Google as an example: the company's valuation doesn't yet reflect revenue—it reflects the credibility of a long-term contracted offtake agreement with a creditworthy buyer. Stina Brock '01, TH'02, Irving Institute Advisory Board member. | Photo by Naomi Wade. Data Centers Cannot Wait for Grid Modernization Much of the discussion circled back to the surging power demand from AI data centers, and how near-term competition for speed to power is pushing developers toward fossil-fuel-based solutions. Interconnection queues now stretch five to nine years, and no data center developer is willing to wait that long. The result is a proliferation of behind-the-meter bridging solutions—often gas turbines—brought in as stopgaps while developers wait for grid connections. One panelist warned this could mean three to five years of elevated carbon intensity, using infrastructure "built to last" for what's meant to be a temporary fix. They suggested the need to design flexible, fungible physical assets, such as turbines that can be redeployed elsewhere, rather than building another generation of assets that may become stranded or delay the transition to low-carbon electricity. The panelists also grappled with the deeper structural challenge of remaking an electricity system built for a different era. Once steel and concrete go into the ground, they tend to stay for decades, and much of the existing system still runs through utilities designed around centralized, one-way power flow. Distributed energy resources—such as rooftop solar, battery storage, and demand response programs—offer one path toward a grid that can flex and rebalance as demand patterns shift. (From left) Geoff Parker and Charlie Donovan. | Photo by Naomi Wade. Capital and the Need for New Thinking An audience member with decades of experience in energy efficiency pushed the panelists on whether capital markets are even asking the right questions. Despite genuine technological progress, the field still treats energy as a commodity to be bought and sold by the unit, rather than a service delivered to meet human needs. They suggested that the structural frameworks shaping capital allocation today are largely holdovers from past decades and should evolve. The panelists largely agreed that this framing problem is real. Capital tends to flow toward what is easiest to measure and price: kilowatt-hours, megawatts, contracted offtake. Rethinking energy in terms of services, rather than units, could unlock different kinds of investment, reward different kinds of performance, and ultimately change what "success" looks like for a project. The panelists acknowledged that meaningful change has occurred within existing frameworks, and that it has been incremental. Whether capital markets are equipped to finance a fundamentally different relationship between energy and its end users remained an open question. The panel closed with a Q&A session with the audience. | Photo by Naomi Wade. The Geopolitics of Cheap Solar Another audience member asked whether Americans should celebrate falling solar costs even when China controls much of the market. Panelists agreed it's both a victory and a strategic vulnerability. Cheap solar panels and EVs accelerate the energy transition everywhere, which is good for global climate goals. But near-total dependence on a geopolitical rival for critical technology inputs is a genuine national security risk that is reshaping geopolitical priorities. The panel closed with a shared recognition that venture capital, late-stage capital, and government support are complementary pieces of an unfinished puzzle—and that solving the "missing middle" is essential to helping promising technologies move from proof of concept to market scale. title: Critical Minerals: The Supply Chain Behind the Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Articles Critical Minerals: The Supply Chain Behind the Energy Transition Image (From left) Roger Ballentine, President of Green Strategies and former Chairman of the White House Climate Change Task Force; Giulia Siccardo, Managing Director and Regional Leader of North America at Quinbrook and a Distinguished Industry Fellow at Dartmouth's Irving Institute; Mansoor Barati, the Gerald R. Heffernan Chair in Materials Processing and Director of the Centre for Metallurgical Processing and Sustainability at the University of Toronto; John Corrigan, Vice President of Policy, Trade, and Industrial Strategy at the Silverado Policy Accelerator; and Danielle Spalding, Senior Vice President of Corporate and External Affairs at Cirba Solutions. (Photo By Eugene Krasnaok) 10/1/2026 Clean energy technologies like solar panels, wind turbines, and batteries are often seen as a clean break from the extractive industries of the fossil fuel era. That perception obscures a basic fact: these technologies depend on critical minerals like lithium, nickel, and cobalt, pulled from the ground just like oil and coal. If the last century of energy and geopolitical policy was shaped by hydrocarbons, the next will be shaped by minerals. That dependence has taken on new urgency as AI data centers, electrification, and the reshoring of manufacturing drive a historic surge in electricity demand. We confront a hard geological reality: the United States does not control the minerals it needs to power its own energy transition. Reconciling that dependency with the urgency of climate change may require the climate movement to make peace with an industry it has long opposed: mining. That's the inconvenient truth that set the tone for a panel convened on September 23 to discuss critical minerals, energy security, and the fragility of the modern energy supply chain. The discussion was held under the Chatham House Rule, so comments below are not attributed to individual speakers. A Panel of Experts The conversation was moderated by Roger Ballentine , President of Green Strategies and former Chairman of the White House Climate Change Task Force under President Clinton. He was joined by four panelists: Giulia Siccardo , Managing Director and Regional Leader of North America at Quinbrook and a Distinguished Industry Fellow at Dartmouth's Irving Institute, who previously led the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Manufacturing and Energy Supply Chains; Mansoor Barati , the Gerald R. Heffernan Chair in Materials Processing and Director of the Centre for Metallurgical Processing and Sustainability at the University of Toronto; John Corrigan , Vice President of Policy, Trade, and Industrial Strategy at the Silverado Policy Accelerator; and Danielle Spalding , Senior Vice President of Corporate and External Affairs at Cirba Solutions, a battery recycling company operating across North America. An audience member asks the panelists a question (left); Roger Ballentine and Giulia Siccardo (top right); John Corrigan and Danielle Spalding (bottom right). | Photos by Eugene Krasnaok. An Expanding Definition of Energy Security The panel opened by redefining the term at the center of the discussion. Energy security used to mean diversifying away from OPEC oil. Today, it also means guaranteeing access to the roughly 50 minerals—lithium, nickel, cobalt, graphite, and rare earth elements—that batteries, magnets, and grid equipment require. According to International Energy Agency estimates, it would take roughly a decade and tens of billions of dollars to build a rare earth supply chain outside of China. That timeline is notably dwarfed by the hundreds of billions of dollars U.S. tech giants are now committing every year to build data centers. The mismatch between how fast mineral supply chains can grow and how fast demand is growing, panelists agreed, is the defining supply chain challenge of this moment. The China Factor Any conversation about critical minerals eventually comes back to China, which controls a majority of the global critical mineral supply chain. China's advantage is both geological and industrial. The country refines an estimated 85 to 90 percent of the world's rare earths and roughly 70 percent of its cobalt, even though it mines only a fraction of global reserves. Panelists stressed that mining is only the first link in a much longer chain, and that the U.S. and its allies need to build refining and processing capacity to build supply chain security. China has tightened export controls, first in 2023 and again through 2025, restricting gallium, germanium (of which it controls roughly 80 percent of global production), and rare earth magnets. Panelists described these moves as calibrated pressure—a way to remind Washington and its allies of their dependence without triggering a full-blown conflict. The goal now, several argued, is to build a functioning "ex-China" market: a trading system among allied nations robust enough that materials can be bought on commercial rather than political terms. An audience member asks the panelists a question (left); and Mansoor Barati (right). | Photos by Eugene Krasnaok. Recycling as the Overlooked Supply Chain While mining takes decades to scale, recycling offers a faster, if partial, fix. The goal, as one panelist put it, is "resilience without reliance." We can recover lithium, nickel, and cobalt from spent batteries and consumer electronics rather than mining new material from the ground. Cirba Solutions recently completed a multiyear qualification process with General Motors that now allows GM to build vehicles using batteries containing recycled cobalt and nickel. Still, recycling is not a complete substitute for mining. On today's trajectory, recycled content could meet about 40 percent of battery material demand by 2040. This leaves a significant gap that virgin extraction must fill. The bottleneck, panelists noted, is not collection but refining capacity. An estimated 85 percent of "black mass"—the shredded material recovered from used batteries—is still processed abroad, much in China. This is where the panel's inconvenient truth came into sharpest focus. If "drill, baby, drill" was the political shorthand of the fossil fuel era, panelists suggested, the clean energy movement may need its own uneasy corollary: "process, baby, process." The point was to acknowledge that batteries, turbines, and solar panels can't be recycled into existence. Some minerals must be mined first. Responsible, well-regulated domestic mining, several panelists agreed, is a precondition for meeting clean energy goals at the speed the transition demands. Capital Is a Real Constraint Geology is one obstacle. Capital is another. Building refining and recycling capacity requires patient capital, and private investors need to see large, reliable offtake agreements before committing funds. Public capital, such as through Department of Energy grants and potentially Pentagon offtake commitments, can de-risk early projects enough to attract private investment. Canada was repeatedly cited as a model of agility, having borrowed elements of U.S. industrial policy while moving faster on permitting and public-private coordination. Critical minerals, several panelists pointed out, currently make up only about a quarter of a battery's total cost. This means that even a significant premium for secure, domestic sourcing may be a price worth paying. Torsten Welte, SVP and General Manager of Energy & Natural Resources Industries at SAP (left); and John Corrigan (right). | Photos by Eugene Krasnaok. Is There a Technological Solution? Can technology simply engineer around scarcity? The panel was skeptical of near-term technological solutions. Battery chemistries do shift over time. For example, natural graphite, still roughly two-thirds sourced from China, is increasingly being replaced with synthetic graphite made from petroleum coke in the U.S. and Canada or silicon. But no chemistry shift eliminates critical mineral dependence outright; it just moves it around. The bigger failure, panelists suggested, is America's inability to scale lab breakthroughs into commercial facilities. This gap was attributed to risk-averse capital markets and thin domestic metallurgical infrastructure. The U.S. holds nickel resources theoretically sufficient for hundreds of millions of electric vehicles, but almost entirely in hard-rock ores that require processing technology the country hasn't scaled up. The Workforce Gap Higher education moves on timescales that don't align with market shifts. Faculty tenure, curriculum approval, and accreditation cycles take years to change, while critical mineral markets shift with each new tariff, export ban, or geopolitical event. The mismatch has left the U.S. without a real pipeline for training accredited mining or metallurgical engineers. Both fields fell out of favor for the same reasons: as U.S. mining and heavy manufacturing declined starting in the 1980s, enrollment dropped, accreditation became harder to justify, and universities redirected resources toward computer science and other higher-demand majors. The result is a talent gap at every level. On the trades side, the reshoring of manufacturing and the buildout of grid infrastructure have created acute shortages of welders and electricians, rooted in the decline of vocational and apprenticeship programs in U.S. high schools over decades. On the engineering side, the industry needs chemical and mining/metallurgical engineers who understand both the theory and the practical challenges of building and operating rare earth refining and battery recycling facilities. There are efforts to narrow the gap. The Department of Energy-backed Battery Workforce Initiative, launched in 2022 with automakers and community colleges, trains workers for battery manufacturing roles. But that doesn't touch the upstream mining, refining, or metallurgical expertise the broader supply chain requires. The U.S. needs to build three distinct talent pipelines at once—skilled trades, process engineering, and extractive metallurgy—using an education system that spent the last forty years dismantling all three. An audience member listens left); and Danielle Spalding (right). | Photos by Eugene Krasnaok. Strategic Solutions Asked about stockpiling minerals the way nations once stockpiled oil, the panel was unenthusiastic. Many processed minerals degrade over time, and government warehousing is a blunt instrument compared to functioning markets. The more elegant fix, several suggested, isn't a strategic reserve but a strategic mindset: treating critical minerals not as commodities to trade opportunistically, but as the foundation of national industrial strategy that is as fundamental to national security as energy itself. The panel closed without resolving the tension it opened with: whether America can align permitting timelines, capital markets, and workforce development quickly enough to match the pace of surging energy demand. But the inconvenient truth the panel started with only grew sharper by the end: there is no clean energy transition without expanded mining and recycling processes, and the movement that has long opposed extraction may have to make peace with it. Anderson Jr. '84, Irving Institute Advisory Board Member (top right); Irving Institute Advisory Board Members Raymond Wood '84, Hilary C. Tompkins '90, H'19, and Matt LeBlanc '92 (bottom right). | Photos by Eugene Krasnaok. title: Advisory Council Forms to Support Climate Collaborative | Dartmouth
text: More news Articles Advisory Council Forms to Support Climate Collaborative News subtitle The group will coordinate activities around climate and sustainability across campus. Image Image A sign on campus about Dartmouth’s decarbonization efforts signals a “greener future in progress.” (Photo by Katie Lenhart) 6/19/2024 More Reading Dartmouth to Invest $500 Million in Decarbonization Body The Dartmouth Climate Collaborative Advisory Council —part of the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative announced this spring to address climate change and sustainability on campus and beyond—will hold its first meeting this summer. “There are many groups on campus working on issues related to climate and sustainability,” says Council Co-Chair Laura Ogden , who is also leading the year-long Climate Futures Initiative that is identifying opportunities for Dartmouth to pursue climate scholarship and education locally, regionally, nationally, and internationally. “This council is charged with taking a big-picture view of the entire ecosystem of climate work at Dartmouth and finding ways, collectively, to elevate that work and make connections that create greater impact.” The council is forming as installation begins this month on the infrastructure that will enable Dartmouth’s campus to transition from steam to hot-water heating, powered by geo-exchange technology—work that is a crucial step toward realizing the Climate Collaborative’s goal of reducing carbon emissions on campus by 60% by 2030 and 100% by 2050. Quote This council is charged with taking a big-picture view of the entire ecosystem of climate work at Dartmouth and finding ways, collectively, to elevate that work. Attribution Laura Ogden, co-chair, Dartmouth Climate Collaborative Advisory Council The advisory council reports to Provost David Kotz ’86 and to Josh Keniston , senior vice president of capital planning and campus operations, and is made up of faculty, students, alumni, and a representative from the community group Sustainable Hanover. It will meet at least quarterly to provide feedback on Dartmouth’s climate and sustainability strategies and to help foster connections with groups across campus and with the Upper Valley community, alumni, and businesses. “We want the council to be inclusive, transparent, and responsive to the community’s interests and needs,” says Co-Chair Rosi Kerr ’97 , director of the Sustainability Office , who says that, among other activities, the group is planning to run focus groups with key constituencies as it begins its work over the summer. In addition to Kerr and Ogden, council members are Bea Burack ’25; Judith Colla, from Sustainable Hanover; Dan Kalafatas ’96, an advisory board member of the Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy and Society; Meredith Kelly, chair of the Department of Earth Sciences; Lindsay Lu ’26; Justin Mankin, associate professor of geography; Geoffrey Parker, professor of engineering and interim director of the Irving Institute; John Sterman ’77, volunteer leader of Dartmouth’s Our Green Future 2.0 and a professor of management at MIT’s Sloan School of Management; Hilary Tompkins ’90, member of the Dartmouth Board of Trustees and a partner with Hogan Lovells; and a graduate student representative to be named. Written by Office of Communications Share this Facebook X Email News contact The Office of Communications can be reached at office.of.communications@dartmouth.edu .
