the Arctic Professors Charlie Donovan - Clinical Professor Melody Brown Burkins - Adjunct Professor; Director, Institute of Arctic Studies Dates November 2026 Destination Cities Copenhagen, Denmark and Helsinki, Finland Course Description Denmark and Finland are often held up as global exemplars of stability, sustainability, and good governance. As Arctic nations, Denmark and Finland also sit at the front lines of a rapidly transforming region where climate change, geopolitical competition, Indigenous rights, and resource extraction are increasingly intertwined. Students on this GIX will explore how capital is being mobilized to support infrastructure development and innovation in the European Arctic region, while simultaneously learning how heightened security concerns and evolving international alliances pose unprecedented challenges. Students will engage directly with leaders of multinational firms and financial institutions working in the two Arctic nations, learning how they are managing emerging trends in climate finance, sustainable development, and the complex geopolitics shaping the Arctic’s economic future. The trip will also highlight Inuit- and Sámi-led perspectives on development, sovereignty, and land use. As renewed great-power competition and accelerating demand for Arctic resources creates new financial opportunities and risks, Denmark and Finland’s approaches to governance and sustainable investment offer models for thought and dialogue. Students will leave better equipped to assess risk, opportunity, and responsibility in global markets where climate change, human rights, and security dynamics are redefining best practices for sustainable economic growth. 100 Tuck Hall Hanover, NH 03755 USA Center for Business, Government & Society Glassmeyer/McNamee Center for Digital Strategies Center for Entrepreneurship Center for Health Care Center for Private Equity and Venture Capital Revers Center for Energy, Sustainability and Innovation Apply Admissions Financial Aid Application Deadlines Admissions FAQs Contact Getting Here See Our Campus Area Lodging Give to Tuck MyTuck for Alumni TuckStuff Store TuckConnect Intranet Employment For Recruiters For Journalists Brand Guidelines Instagram LinkedIn YouTube Back to Top © , The Trustees of Dartmouth College.. title: South America Projects — Energy Justice Clinic
text: South America Projects Through collaborative research with affected communities and specialists, we focus on how Indigenous in Walmapu, Chile, and Latin America are being recognized in the energy transition. Trajectory Our long-term case collaboration is with the Pilmaiken territory over a transnational hydropower conflict on Mapuche-Williche Indigenous lands in Chile. This brought three members of the team to Norway in May 2023 to observe and provide technical support for Mapuche-Williche leaders seeking to halt energy development on their sacred river. Dartmouth students conduct independent research as part of the Energy Justice Clinic with communities in Brazil, Colombia, and Peru. Hydropower Conflict Involving Statkraft Building on Professor Sarah Kelly's decade-long work with the Mapuche-Williche Indigenous community, we study an enduring conflict between Mapuche-Williche communities, a Norwegian state-owned renewable energy company, Statkraft, and the Chilean state. Working with Mapuche-Williche communities and an international network of collaborators, the Clinic has developed timelines of the conflict based on Indigenous perspectives of time according to non-linearity. The Clinic has produced a report on the case, theorizing through the lens of energy justice, legal studies, and Indigenous sovereignty about the disruption of this Global North company on Indigenous cosmovisions and territorial relationships in the Global South. In an effort involving scholars from Brazil, Colombia, Chile, Norway, and the United States, we have analyzed how Statkraft is blatantly disregarding several of the United Nations Guiding Principles for Business and Human Rights and the International Labor Organization Convention 169. Our research centers on how Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) is enacted in practice, which is a critical legal mechanism for Indigenous rights internationally. Through our collaborative research, we aim to decolonize what we consider legitimate practices of knowledge production. For example, to question what we mean by "energy", "justice" and "sovereignty" – and who consolidated such definitions in the first place. Such questioning opens up possibilities to validate, for instance, Indigenous cosmovisions that place nature as part of kinship relationshipsinstead of as natural resources. Therefore, it becomes feasible to support these historically marginalized communities to reclaim their narratives, territories, and ways of living. title: Miranda Ballentine | Climate Collaborative
text: Miranda Ballentine Appointments Distinguished Industry Fellow Biography The Honorable Miranda Ballentine serves as a Distinguished Industry Fellow at the Irving Institute for Energy & Society, where she plays a pivotal role in advancing the Institute's mission across our research, teaching, and engagement programs. With expertise spanning corporate, government, and nonprofit sectors, she supports the Institute's efforts to cultivate a multidisciplinary community dedicated to the decarbonization of the global economy. Ballentine is devoted to accelerating clean energy initiatives for national security, economic prosperity, and solving climate change. Recognized among the 100 most influential climate leaders on the inaugural TIME100 CLIMATE list, she has a proven record of successfully launching and overseeing clean energy strategies at executive levels across sectors. Ballentine was the founding CEO of the Clean Energy Buyers Alliance (CEBA), where she built a community of corporate energy customers to enhance their impact on grid decarbonization. During her six-year tenure, she established CEBA as the leading voice of energy customer companies, contributing to over 30% of added clean energy capacity in the United States. Prior to entrepreneurship, Miranda was an intrapreneur with the nation's two largest energy customers. In 2014, appointed by President Obama and confirmed by the U.S. Senate, she served as the 4th Assistant Secretary of the Air Force (Installations, Environment, & Energy), managing a $9 billion energy budget and launching the Resilient Energy Demonstration Initiative focused on cyber-secure microgrids Previously, as Director of Sustainability for Global Renewable Energy at Walmart, she led initiatives across 15 countries, identifying over $1 billion in potential annual energy savings and significant reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. Her career also includes roles as CEO of Constant Power, Inc., Managing Director of Rocky Mountain Institute's Business Renewables Center (which became CEBA), and Vice President at David Gardiner & Associates. Ballentine is the inaugural Board Chair of the Foundation for Energy, Security, and Innovation (FESI) and co-chairs the Aspen Energy Policy Forum . She is also involved with the Strategic Advisory Committee for Idaho National Lab and serves on several advisory boards, including Greenbelt Capital Partners , the Electric Infrastructure Security Council , and the Center for Climate and Energy Security . In 2013, she was selected as a World Economic Forum Young Global Leader , and in 2020 she was honored as Woman of the Year by the Women's Council on Environment and Energy . Awarded the Air Force's highest civilian honors, she holds a BS magna cum laude from Colorado State University and an MBA from George Washington University, specializing in energy, environmental management, and international business. title: Melody Brown Burkins | Climate Collaborative
text: Melody Brown Burkins Adjunct Professor Appointments Director, Institute of Arctic Studies Sr Assoc Director, John Sloan Dickey Center for International Understanding UArctic Chair in Science Diplomacy and Inclusion Fellow, International Science Council (FISC) Area of Expertise Arctic & Polar Science Diplomacy , Global Science Policy & Diplomacy , Inclusive Governance , Earth & Environmental Science , Strategic Planning & Partnerships , Leadership & Experiential Education , Sustainable Development Biography Melody Brown Burkins, PhD, is the Director of the Institute of Arctic Studies , Senior Associate Director in the John Sloan Dickey Center for International Understanding , and Adjunct Professor of Environmental Studies at Dartmouth. In January 2022, she was also named the UArctic Chair in Science Diplomacy and Inclusion at Dartmouth and also serves on the UArctic academic advisory board, Mimir . With over 30 years of experience as a polar scientist working in academia and governance, she is an advocate for policy-engaged scholarship, experiential education, and the support of science policy and diplomacy initiatives advancing sustainability, inclusive governance, and gender equality in the Arctic and around the world. A "science diplomat" for Arctic and global issues, Dr. Burkins currently serves as a member of the International Steering Committee for the 4th International Conference on Arctic Research Planning (ICARPIV) and the Planning Group for the 5th International Polar Year (IPY-5). She also serves on the UN Office of Disaster Risk Reduction Global Assessment Report (UNDRR-GAR) Advisory Board and is a Fellow of the International Science Council (ISC) . She is a former Chair of both the U.S. National Academies' Board on International Scientific Organizations (BISO) and US National Committee for the International Union of Geological Sciences (USNC-IUGS) . In 2020-2022, she was honored to serve on the 15-Member UNESCO Global Independent Expert Group on Universities and the 2030 Agenda (EGU2030) and, with her international co-authors, publish the 2022 UNESCO report: Knowledge-driven actions: transforming higher education for global sustainability. Her work to advance science policy and diplomacy in the North and globally informs her teaching at Dartmouth ( ENVS62: The Practice of Science Policy and Diplomacy ), where she challenges students to consider how we ensure the most robust, inclusive & ethical knowledge systems are applied to pressing global challenges, be it climate change or the ethical development and engagement of AI. Committed to the support of next generation thought-leaders in sustainability and inclusion, she believes the work requires prioritizing and incentivizing community-engaged academic collaborations, the respect of diverse knowledge systems and Indigenous Peoples' rights in scholarship and policy, and supporting international efforts to inform and advance the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs ). Born and raised in Fairbanks, Alaska, Dr. Burkins' strong personal and professional connections to the North also inform her work to connect Dartmouth students and faculty with opportunities for Arctic scholarship, international cooperation, and policy engagement. She leads the UArctic Institute for Arctic Policy and serves as Vice Lead of the UArctic Model Arctic Council Thematic Network (TN) . In 2018, she had the honor of serving as a formal UArctic Observer to the SDWG and SAO Arctic Council meetings in Rovaniemi, Finland . Burkins is also an advocate for US-Canada collaborations and programs in the Arctic and globally. In 2017, she worked with Alaskan and Canadian colleagues to host the first US-Canada Arctic Science Diplomacy and Leadership Workshop and, in 2018, created an innovative Arctic science diplomacy workshop with McGill's Science & Policy Exchange . She served as a science policy advisor to the first Fulbright Arctic Initiative (FAI) meeting in Iqaluit, Nunavut, in 2015 and continues to engage with FAI cohorts as they advance timely, policy-relevant Arctic knowledge for decision-makers. She enjoys sharing the experience of developing and leading effective science policy and diplomacy collaborations with colleagues and students at Dartmouth and around the world in talks, webinars, workshops, and panel discussions. Burkins' early career as a polar geoscientist expanded to science policy and diplomacy when she was awarded the 1999-2000 AAAS Congressional Science and Technology Policy Fellowship sponsored by the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) and Geological Society of America (GSA). Drawn to policy-making and informed advocacy, she worked briefly as a AAAS Congressional Fellow in Washington, D.C., before accepting a formal position as the energy and environment policy advisor to U.S. Senator Patrick Leahy from Vermont. In that role, she helped advance federal policies for sustainable energy, forestry, agriculture, and conservation practices. Returning north in 2002 with a young family, she spent over a decade at the University of Vermont (UVM) in a diversity of leadership and management roles. This included serving as director of the Northeastern States Research Cooperative , executive director of the Vermont Monitoring Cooperative , associate dean in the College of Engineering and Mathematical Sciences , UVM director of federal relations , interim director of the UVM supercomputing facility , and senior director for research and strategic initiatives - including the UVM Transdisciplinary Research Initiatve (TRI) - through 2014. She was the recipient of a 2013 HERS Fellowship for women leaders in higher education and co-edited a book of invited essays, Holistic Engineering Education: Beyond Technology (Springer, 2010) , about the future of more inclusive engineering education and practice. Burkins' work in both academic and policy leadership roles has led to multiple international appointments by the U.S. National Academy of Sciences. In 2016, she was the first woman to chair a U.S. delegation to an International Geological Congress (34th IGC, South Africa), creating the first majority-female delegation of U.S. geoscience leaders. In 2016, she served on the global ICSU-ISSC Strategy Working Group to connect scientific organizations across the natural, physical, and social sciences and create the first International Science Council. She has also served as an scholar-delegate for Dartmouth in the advancement of Arctic scholarship and cooperation, most recently, at the 2025 UArctic Assembly in Inari, Sapmi, Finland . Burkins also believes in the importance of service to her community and state. She served on the State of Vermont's first Comprehensive Economic Development Strategy (CEDS) committee in 2014, the Board of Vermont's Energy Action Network (EAN) from 2012 to 2015, the Board of Trustees for Vermont's oldest secondary school, Thetford Academy from 2017-2021, and the Advisory Council of Emerge Vermont, encouraging women's political leadership and voice (2015-2020). Burkins earned her B.S. in geology at Yale and both her M.S. and Ph.D. at Dartmouth, focusing her doctoral studies on earth and ecosystem studies in the Antarctic Dry Valleys . She lives in East Thetford, Vermont, with her husband, two sons, and happy dog. View More Education Ph.D. Dartmouth M.S. Dartmouth B.S. text: Giulia Siccardo '12 Appointments Distinguished Industry Fellow Biography As a Distinguished Industry Fellow at the Irving Institute for Energy & Society, Giulia Siccardo '12 plays a critical role in advancing the Institute's research and translation, teaching and learning, and engagement agenda. Her interdisciplinary expertise and cross-sectoral leadership experience support the Irving Institute's efforts to promote entrepreneurship, engage industry, and forge lasting partnerships. Siccardo is an experienced professional in the energy, automotive, and sustainability sectors. She currently serves as Managing Director at Quinbrook Infrastructure Parners, where she leads the North Amarica investment team advancing critical infrastructure for renewable and carbon-free power solutions. Siccardo joined Quinbrook from the U.S. Department of Energy where she was the inaugural Director of the Office of Manufacturing & Energy Supply Chains (MESC). There, she was responsible for awarding tens of billions of dollars in government investments to strengthen and secure U.S. manufacturing capacity and workforce development, as well as administering the Defense Production Act for critical energy technologies. Her scope included batteries, hydrogen, heat pumps, solar, transmission, and zero-emission materials, among other technologies. Siccardo helped launch the Mapping, Modeling, and Analysis Consortium (MMAC), a partnership between MESC and DOE's National Labs to further strategic energy supply chain analysis for DOE, the National Security Council, and other interagency and allied partner organizations. Siccardo was previously a Partner at McKinsey & Company, leading McKinsey's Green Growth work. For over a decade there, she focused on scaling low-carbon systems and value chains across major corporations and emerging start-ups, covering zero-emissions energy, vehicles, and materials. In addition to her scale-up work, Siccardo fostered new ways for corporations to work together to signal demand for emerging clean energy technology. While with McKinsey, she co-founded Frontier, a $1B+ advance market commitment by industry-leading corporations to catalyze high-permanence carbon dioxide removals. Siccardo previously worked at Adobe on clean energy procurement and data center decarbonization. Throughout her career, she's been recognized for her leadership in advancing women in the energy, automotive & sustainability sectors. Born in California, Siccardo holds a dual B.A. in Economics and Environmental Studies from Dartmouth College and an MBA from Harvard Business School. View More Contact Giulia.Siccardo@dartmouth.edu

title: Energy Ventures | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Energy Ventures Dartmouth's Irving Institute Energy Ventures program offers a comprehensive experience from concept to market, designed to empower the next generation of energy and climate entrepreneurs. This program provides a systematic approach and methodology, enabling students and researchers to develop and launch impactful solutions and ventures. Engagement Additional navigation Close Engagement and Collaboration Climate Week NYC Energy Ventures Alumni Three Terms: Fall '26, Winter '27, and Spring '27 Registration for the 2026-2027 academic year will open in October 2026. Selected teams will have the chance to participate in paid Venture-Build Internships during the summer of 2027. Our inaugural program in the 2025-2026 academic year attracted over 100 participants, including Dartmouth undergraduates, graduate students, and postdocs. They learned to build and launch scalable ventures addressing critical energy transition and climate challenges. Join us for an Info Session to learn more! Energy Ventures Info Session Wednesday, October 21 6 - 7 pm Murdough — Third floor MEM space — Accessible from the second floor of the Irving Institute Pizza will be provided! Registration required. Open to: Dartmouth undergraduates, graduate students, and postdocs. Register for the Info Session Register for the Info Session Program Goal & Approach Energy Ventures exists to equip you with the mindset, knowledge, and skills to systematically build, test, and launch business ventures capable of transforming the energy and climate landscape. Our approach is grounded in proven entrepreneurial principles with real-world execution. You'll learn by doing — inside a community built to support bold ideas and ambitious builders. To achieve that, we provide: Home base and community: A "place to go" - a collaborative, cross-disciplinary environment where you can test concepts, challenge assumptions, access cross-disciplinary talent, and build alongside peers who push your thinking and support your progress. A rigorous, applied curriculum: A disciplined, end-to-end process for venture creation. You'll learn the methodology, tools, and techniques required to systematically identify real opportunities, validate customer needs, prototype solutions, design sustainable business models, and begin scaling with confidence. Coaching from real builders: Dedicated, hands-on support from experienced entrepreneurs, product builders, designers, engineers, and investors who know what it takes to refine, test, and launch commercially viable innovations. Program Structure & Progression Energy Ventures covers the entire venture creation process – from generating and refining ideas to building viable products, services, and scalable business ventures. I. Foundations A three-term experience designed to build your entrepreneurial foundations and momentum. Focus: Develop the mindset, knowledge, and skills and tactics essential for early-stage venture creation. Learn foundational methods, tools, and techniques — and immediately apply them to your venture. Activities: Weekly training modules, hands-on workshops, expert coaching, and dedicated mentorship. II. Summer Accelerator (Summer 2027 Term) A full-time, immersive accelerator designed to rapidly advance the most promising teams. Purpose: Fast-track venture through deep customer discovery, rapid prototyping, and business model refinement. Incentive: Teams selected for this phase receive paid internships to work on their ventures full-time. Activities: Continued weekly training, high-frequency workshops, tailored coaching, and close mentorship from industry experts. Program Education, Training, and Mentorship Energy Ventures is led by Josh Creamer, Head of Entrepreneurship at the Irving Institute, alongside other seasoned product builders, designers, engineers, and investors. This group brings deep, real-world venture-building expertise — ensuring every participant is guided by practitioners who have built, launched, and scaled successful ventures. Participants also gain access to an exceptional network of mentors—leaders who have founded companies, shaped industries, and turned bold ideas into impact. These mentors will provide hands-on coaching, strategic guidance, and real-world perspective throughout the journey. This network surrounds participants with the expertise, credibility, and support needed to accelerate your ventures. Frequently Asked Questions If you don't see an answer to your question below, please reach out to us at Energy.Ventures@dartmouth.edu . Is there a cost for the program? No, there is no cost to participate in Energy Ventures. Will modules and lectures be online or in person? The modules and lectures will be in person for all participants. There will be weekly sessions. Can alumni participate? Alumni can participate on a team, as long as there is at least one current Dartmouth student, postdoc, faculty or staff member on the team as well. The alumni will also need to attend the weekly sessions in person, as a large component of this program is team-building. This is best done in person!

title: What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Articles What It Takes to Build a Community-Centered Energy Transition Image (From left) Sarah Kelly, head of Dartmouth's Energy Justice Clinic; Jasmine Graham, executive director of Mid-Hudson Energy Transition; and Mark James, director of the Institute for Energy and the Environment at Vermont Law and Graduate School.  (Photo By Naomi Wade) 9/25/2026 The energy transition is underway, but its path is uneven and shrouded in fog. Whether that transition ultimately distributes benefits fairly, respects the people it affects, and builds lasting power within local communities, depends on the choices made along the way. That distinction was central to a Sept. 22 panel hosted by the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative during Climate Week NYC on what it takes to advance an affordable, community-centered energy transition. A Panel of Experts Sarah Kelly , head of Dartmouth's Energy Justice Clinic, moderated a wide-ranging conversation with Jasmine Graham , executive director of Mid-Hudson Energy Transition, and Mark James , director of the Institute for Energy and the Environment at Vermont Law and Graduate School. Together, the practitioners, who work across community organizing, legal advocacy, and academia, explored how communities can be the visionaries and primary beneficiaries of their energy futures. What emerged was a set of provocative ideas and hard-won lessons about what building a genuinely community-centered energy transition actually requires. Justice Is Multifaceted The panel opened by outlining a framework for energy justice built on four complementary components: Distributive Justice: Who bears the benefits and burdens of new energy infrastructure? Recognition Justice: Are we acknowledging the unique energy needs, vulnerabilities, and contributions of community members rather than marginalizing communities from energy planning? Restorative Justice: Are we actively remediating burdens already inflicted, not just preventing future harm? Procedural Justice: Who holds decision-making authority, and what scaffolding exists to meaningfully engage communities in that process? Procedural justice—involving communities in decisions about what gets sited where and which solutions get prioritized—came up repeatedly. Speakers noted that decisions about energy infrastructure have historically been made behind closed doors by a small set of powerful interests. A prime example is how fossil fuel infrastructure has often ended up where communities have had the least power and the least voice. Without procedural justice, panelists argued, the other three dimensions struggle to gain purchase. While the energy transition itself was described as a shift "from molecules to electrons," the justice component was framed as a parallel shift in power. It requires moving decision-making authority away from concentrated interests and toward the people most directly affected by energy choices. Audience members chat with panelists, including Mark James, director of the Institute for Energy and the Environment at Vermont Law and Graduate School (right). | Photo by Naomi Wade. Ownership as a Mechanism If procedural justice is the guiding principle, ownership emerged as the practical mechanism for realizing it. Speakers underscored that participation without ownership is not enough. It is ownership that transforms a community from subject to stakeholder. Panelists offered several examples: One community-based energy transition included a community energy council that meets monthly to set priorities, build shared understanding, and work through challenges via an iterative process before launching new projects. That same initiative created a community investment fund with a new loan product, reserving board seats for a community investor and a loan-program borrower. Including a borrower on the board ensures the lending product stays responsive to the people actually using it. Another initiative launched a community-owned solar project in a major urban area that will return more than $1 million into a community resiliency fund for future climate projects. The project will also save participating families around 20% on their electricity bills and benefit local small businesses. A technical assistance project helped a local government develop zoning bylaws to support a battery storage proposal in a community that had no such bylaws in place. Trust Is Built in Years and Destroyed in Seconds A recurring theme was how much time, care, and communication is required to earn community trust, and how quickly that trust can be lost. One example underscored the point vividly: a community solar program in which participants saw only a marginal discount on their electric bills, and only after 9 to 14 months of being subscribed. Residents who had signed up 10 months earlier with no visible benefit grew frustrated and distrustful, forcing the program to pause new subscriptions to avoid further eroding community trust. As one speaker put it: trust "takes a long time to build and seconds to destroy." (From left) Meredith Kelly, faculty director of the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative, and Christa Daniels, assistant director for community partnerships with the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative. | Photo by Naomi Wade. Communication as Core Infrastructure Panelists agreed that consistent, thoughtful communication is central to build trust and drive action. Tactics discussed included: Bilingual outreach to translate technical jargon, both linguistically and conceptually. Naming matters: One home upgrade program initially branded around "health and resilience" gained no traction. Once rebranded with a simpler, warmer name, "hug," it was embraced. Meeting people in their own space and time: Rather than asking community members to come to institutions, some speakers emphasized going directly into communities, including on weekends. Sharing struggle, as well as solutions: Communities are already accustomed to talking about problems; a speaker noted that it's truly energizing for residents to talk about solutions instead. Right-Sized, Not Scaled Up A strong theme running through the panel was a challenge to the default instinct toward scale. "Sometimes we shouldn't scale up," one speaker argued. "A just, community-based, renewable energy transition doesn't have to scale." Drawing on Amory Lovins' The Road Not Taken, panelists suggested the goal is to bring technology "down to the right size, " whether that means how a household heats water or how a town builds a thermal energy network. This resistance to scale connected to a broader concern about concentrated control over resources, with several speakers calling for greater modularity, diversity, and a "hubs and nodes" model rather than hierarchical oversight. Community solar and thermal energy networks were repeatedly cited as technologies suited to this right-sized approach, for example, geothermal systems that deliver heat at useful temperatures, modeled at municipal or neighborhood scale. The Money Problem Asked what single thing they would change, panelists agreed on funding. Current philanthropic and grant models are project-based and cyclical, forcing leaders to spend enormous time fundraising rather than building. The proposed alternative: unrestricted general operating support. This means large flexible pools of capital that communities could draw against based on their own determination of need, rather than funders' predefined categories. A related theme concerned how benefits get counted. One speaker called for broadening cost-benefit analysis: rather than measuring a clean energy intervention by bill savings alone, calculate its cascading benefits on nutrition, education, hospital utilization, and food security. Demonstrating the full breadth of benefits, the argument went, builds not just an ethical case but a "systems-wide logic" case. An expanded understanding of benefits could generate the political momentum needed for widespread deployment of technologies that already exist. Before and after the panel, guests were invited to view research posters and discuss projects with Dartmouth undergraduate students. | Photo by Naomi Wade. Conclusion: A Test of Commitment The panel closed by returning to where it began: the energy transition is inevitable, but justice is not. Whether that transition rebalances who holds ownership, who is trusted to lead, what counts as success, and where capital flows depends on the choices made along the way. Communities, speakers emphasized, already know what they need. The remaining questions are whether institutions, funders, and outside experts are willing to be genuine partners with the frontline communities they aim to serve—or whether they'll default to convention simply because it's familiar. The well-worn path is often less durable and less equitable. Centering communities in decision-making and ownership is what makes the transition more likely to last. Written by Cate Homicki & Adamari Benavidez Share this Tags Dartmouth Climate Collaborative

Led by Professor Laura Ogden , former Special Advisor to the Provost on Climate and Sustainability, the Climate Futures Initiative identified Dartmouth's distinct strengths in climate research and teaching and made recommendations to help amplify those strengths. Read the Climate Futures Initiative Final Report and Appendices to learn more. To carry the work of the Climate Futures Initiative forward, Professor Meredith Kelly has been appointed as Faculty Director of the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative and will co-chair the Dartmouth Climate Collaborative Advisory Council with Director of Sustainability Rosi Kerr ’97 . title: Executive Director Named for New Black Cultural Institute | Dartmouth
text: More news Articles Executive Director Named for New Black Cultural Institute News subtitle Other new hires include a special advisor on climate and a director of federal relations. Image Image From left, Laura Ogden, David Robinson-Morris, and Emily Burlij. (Illustration by Erin Supinka) 2/2/2024 More Reading New Hub for Black Intellectual and Cultural Life Launches Body Dartmouth filled some key positions in January in the Institute for Black Intellectual and Cultural Life , the Office of the Provost , and the Office of Government and Community Relations . David W. Robinson-Morris Executive Director, Institute for Black Intellectual and Cultural Life The Institute for Black Intellectual and Cultural Life has hired David Robinson-Morris as its first executive director, beginning Jan. 22. Robinson-Morris joins Director Kimberly Juanita Brown , an associate professor of English and creative writing, in the leadership of the institute, which launched last summer as a cultural and scholarly hub for the Black community at Dartmouth. As executive director, Robinson-Morris is working alongside Brown to provide leadership for the institute. “I am so thrilled to join the Dartmouth community and to lead the institute—which was catalyzed by Black alumni and friends of Dartmouth—alongside Kimberly Juanita Brown,” Robinson-Morris says. “The institute invites us into a long, rich intellectual tradition of wrestling with ideas from diverse Black and African diasporic perspectives. We seek to build upon the ideas of past and present Black thinkers and artists, generate new understandings, and imagine liberated futures to solve contemporary dis-ease. Our work—our programming, our thinking, and our reimagining of the world—must necessarily unfurl toward liberation, justice, and collective transformation.” Quote The institute invites us into a long, rich intellectual tradition of wrestling with ideas from diverse Black and African diasporic perspectives. Attribution David Robinson-Morris, executive director, Institute for Black Intellectual and Cultural Life The author of Ubuntu and Buddhism in Higher Education: An Ontological (Re)Thinking , as well as several peer-reviewed articles, Robinson-Morris is the founder and chief of the strategic diversity, equity, and inclusion consultancy The ReImaginelution. Previously, he was executive director of the Center for Contemplative Mind in Society; regional director of diversity and inclusion of the Bayou Region for Ochsner Health; founding director of the Center for Equity, Justice, and the Human Spirit; and an assistant professor in the Division of Education and Counseling at Xavier University of Louisiana, where he served as assistant vice president of development. He completed his bachelor’s degree in communications and public relations at Loyola University New Orleans and went on to earn a master’s of public administration from the University of New Orleans and a PhD in educational leadership and research from Louisiana State University, where he also earned a certificate as an education specialist. His doctoral dissertation won the 2016 American Association of Blacks in Higher Education Dissertation Award. In addition to Robinson-Morris, Jénee Potts has joined the institute as program coordinator. Laura Ogden Special Advisor to the Provost on Climate and Sustainability Professor of Anthropology Laura Ogden has been named to a new, one-year advisory role designed to “enable Dartmouth to maximize its academic impact in the climate space and to help identify ways to support that work in the future,” according to an announcement on the Office of the Provost website . Action on climate change is one of the top priorities that President Sian Leah Beilock outlined in her inaugural address . “This year, I will be convening interdisciplinary conversations on campus to help identify Dartmouth’s unique strengths and opportunities for climate scholarship and teaching, beginning with the question of how best to activate our amazing resources, such as forest lands, our organic farm, and the campus itself,” Ogden says. “Of course, we need to balance a careful and inclusive approach to understanding these opportunities with the urgency we all feel about climate change. Therefore, I will also work with the provost to identify projects and initiatives that we can begin this year, including those focused on engaging our campus and Upper Valley communities.” As a scholar, Ogden studies the politics of environmental change and conservation. Her work includes ethnographic research in the Florida Everglades; Tierra del Fuego, Chile; and urban environments around the United States. She is the author of two books, Loss and Wonder at the World’s End and Swamplife: The Entangled Lives of Hunters, Gators and Mangroves in the Florida Everglades. A graduate of the University of North Carolina, she earned her master’s and PhD in anthropology from the University of Florida. She has been a member of the Dartmouth faculty since 2014. Emily Burlij Director of Federal Relations Dartmouth’s Office of Government and Community Relations has appointed Emily Burlij to support Dartmouth’s strategic relationships with federal agencies, policy officials, decision-makers, and thought leaders in Washington, D.C. She will also advise Dartmouth’s leaders on national issues, policies, and regulations. “There is so much potential here at Dartmouth to build its reputation among D.C. audiences as a pioneering research institution,” says Burlij, who will report to Emma Wolfe , the vice president for government and community relations. “I am excited to be joining at such a pivotal time, both at Dartmouth and within the national higher education landscape.” Burlij comes to Dartmouth from Boston University’s Office of Federal Relations, where she spent 11 years, first as associate director and then director. Previously, Burlij was an associate with the lobbying firm Cassidy & Associates, a legislative program assistant for the Natural Resources Defense Council, and a development associate for the National Park Foundation. She graduated from Villanova University with a bachelor’s degree in political science and went on to earn her JD from Washington College of Law at American University. Written by Office of Communications Share this Facebook X Email News contact The Office of Communications can be reached at office.of.communications@dartmouth.edu . title: Courses & Curriculum | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Courses & Curriculum Dartmouth's Master of Energy Transition (MET) curriculum is grounded in interdisciplinary learning, with a consistent emphasis on the energy transition's impact on social systems and community well-being, locally and globally. MET faculty member Cong Chen, Assistant Professor of Engineering, teaches Data Analytics for Energy and Climate (ENTR 140). Education Additional navigation Close Teaching and Learning at the Irving Institute Undergraduate Students Graduate Students Master of Energy Transition Degree Courses & Curriculum MET Faculty Mentorship, Networking & Community Career Treks Alumni & Careers Class of 2026 Profiles Class of 2027 Profiles Info Sessions & Admissions Events Apply to the MET Frequently Asked Questions Energy Justice Clinic Resources Cultivating a Community of Energy Leaders Dartmouth's non-thesis, professional Master of Energy Transition (MET) program prepares you to make an immediate impact in the clean energy transition. With in-person courses on Dartmouth's scenic campus, you'll benefit from meaningful connections with instructors, fellow students, guest speakers, and industry and nonprofit partners, all in a collaborative academic setting. "Our energy systems are the backbone of modern life, and they are under extreme pressure to transform. The challenges this creates do not respect borders of any kind — disciplinary, national, or geographic. It has been a dream to build a program that is laser-focused on increasing society's capacity to not just address these challenges, but to use them as an opportunity to build a better world." — Amanda Graham, PhD, Director of Academic Programs & the MET Course Descriptions The MET program spans three academic terms. During each 10-week term, you'll complete three courses. Our courses are organized into three thematic areas. Technology of Energy Systems Fall Term | ENTR 110: Technology of Current & Future Energy Systems Course description: This course provides an overview of current and emerging technologies spanning the entire energy value chain—from generation to the grid edge. Students will explore a broad range of energy facilities and infrastructure, including traditional systems such as fossil fuels, nuclear power, and large-scale grids, while critically examining the ongoing transition to low-carbon and decentralized energy solutions. Topics include renewable energy integration (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal), smart grids, energy storage, electric vehicles, grid resilience, and next-generation clean energy technologies. Through real-world case studies, simulation exercises, and project-based learning, students will evaluate the trade-offs and system-level implications of various energy pathways. The course prepares students to make meaningful contributions to the development and deployment of resilient, efficient, and sustainable energy systems. Winter Term | ENTR 140: Data Analytics for Energy & Climate Course description: This course provides an introduction to the concepts and applications of data analytics for energy and climate. Topics include data collection and preparation, descriptive statistics, machine learning, optimization, and visualization. The course will introduce the overall process of using data analytics to solve problems, leveraging real-world data related to energy and climate. Students acquire a working knowledge of coding and analytics (Python or similar) with practical datasets related to electricity markets, power system operations, and climate. Spring Term | ENTR 170: Energy Systems Modeling Course description: This course introduces how to use and evaluate computational energy systems models to solve integrated technological, environmental, economic, cultural, and social problems. Foundational models of energy system operations, planning, investment, markets, technology adoption, and trade are introduced. Fundamental systems modeling topics are covered, including the treatment of uncertainty, spatial and temporal scaling, multi-sector dynamics, multi-stakeholder preferences, multiple objectives, and environmental and socioeconomic impacts (e.g., air quality, labor, land use, social equity). Existing, transforming, and emerging systems are explored, such as power, renewable, fossil fuel, hydrogen, carbon capture, transmission, industrial, residential, and transportation systems. Business and Economics of Energy Fall Term | ENTR 120: Team Dynamics & Professional Communications Course description: The evolving energy and climate workplace requires sophisticated professional skills. This course will serve as a laboratory for honing those skills in order to successfully pursue and perform in a meaningful career in the energy transition. Students will identify and apply core principles of teamwork, leadership, and communication, and will expand their ability to leverage skills in these areas to facilitate professional success. The course will include workshops and mentorship in career self-assessment, ethics, and interpersonal and organizational communication. Winter Term | ENTR 150: Energy Markets & Economics Course description: This course provides the conceptual and applied foundation in energy economics necessary to engage with the market frameworks at work in multiple sectors of the energy economy. Students will explore key aspects of energy supply and demand and assess the role of markets, regulation and deregulation in energy systems. The course addresses market design questions related to energy generation, transmission and distribution. It also provides an overview of economic institutions designed to control the impacts of energy infrastructure and examines market innovations that can advance energy policy goals and accelerate decarbonization. Spring Term | ENTR 180: Finance & Accounting for the Energy Transition Course description: The energy transition is a massive undertaking requiring trillions of dollars of investment. This course will explore concepts from finance and accounting that are crucial to understanding the rationale for investment decision-making.  We will work with various methods for assessing the financial viability of energy and decarbonization projects and managing financial risks. Critical topics that will be addressed include discounted cashflow modelling, financial & carbon accounting, investment risk analysis, & project financing. We will also explore ongoing innovations that seek to establish the next generation of financial products, services, and institutions that can effectively serve the goals of the energy transition. Students will develop both tactical and strategic skills to help them manage the financial aspects of energy projects, with the goal of becoming confident and conversant about the avenues available for securing commercial & concessional sources of funding. Science, Policy, and Impact of Energy Fall Term | ENTR 130: Climate Science & the Energy Transition Course description: This course will build on the basic principles of climate science to explore drivers of present-day climate change, including greenhouse gasses, and their impacts on society and ecosystems. With an emphasis on project-based learning, students will examine the interactions of climate change and economic growth, and how these affect a society's ability to navigate the energy transition. Critical to evaluate will be the socioecological costs and benefits of climate mitigation measures over short (years to decades) to long (decades to a century) time horizons, and at local to regional to global scales. Winter Term | ENTR 160: Energy Law & Policy Course description: This course will address the evolving U.S. policy context for energy system management and transition. We will briefly review historical approaches to managing energy resources before focusing on recent and emerging governance models as well as regulatory challenges and incentives for the deployment of emerging energy technologies. Throughout the course, we will examine the interplay between technological and social systems, including the key role of technology in both creating and mediating environmental impacts and the roles of policy and politics in shaping technology choices. We will use a diverse set of tools and methodologies to investigate the social and environmental implications of energy technology and policy choice. We will assess how these issues interact at multiple scales, particularly local, state, regional, and national, and review major global trends and their potential impact on U.S. energy law and policy. Spring Term | ENTR 190: Community & Global Resilience in Energy Transitions Course description: This course examines how energy systems and climate impacts reinforce longstanding social and economic inequities. Students will investigate who benefits and who is burdened, historically and today, across local and global contexts. Through a systems thinking lens, students will explore how natural and social systems are interconnected, interdependent, and shaped by dynamic feedback loops. Using this holistic approach, students will assess real-world case studies, identify leverage points for change, and analyze community-level climate and energy strategies from within and beyond the U.S. Emphasizing applied learning, students will engage in collaborative projects and comparative case analysis to develop actionable insights and equity-centered solutions. The course equips students with the systems literacy, effective engagement tools and techniques, and strategic frameworks needed for leadership in the energy transition and climate resilience field. Project-Based Courses Experiential learning is a cornerstone of the MET curriculum. Throughout the program, you'll encounter real-world scenarios in projects of varying scales. In some, you’ll partner with cross-sector organizations committed to decarbonization and sustainability. In all three thematic areas of the curriculum, you will wrestle with the complexity of transforming energy systems large and small—equipping you with skills and insights to directly implement in your career. Cross-sector Communication Skills Even as AI and technical advances transform the workforce, the skills that set professionals apart remain distinctly human: the capacity to work in teams, communicate across differences, and translate complex ideas into meaningful action. This is especially true in the energy sector, where every challenge sits at the intersection of multiple fields. Through our interdisciplinary curriculum, MET students gain fluency in speaking the languages of technology, finance, and policy. We go beyond concepts and theory, anchoring lessons in real-world projects and networking opportunities—because the best way to learn a new language is to speak it in practice. Alongside this fluency, you'll build core professional communication skills and develop your professional persona: practicing presentations, sharpening your interview technique, and learning what it takes to adapt your leadership and work styles in dynamic workplace environments. A Focus on Community Impact The MET program emphasizes equity and justice in how the energy transition affects social systems and communities, locally and globally. Because it's not just about the technology—decarbonization will only succeed if it's affordable, accessible, and fair, and if the people affected by it have a voice in shaping it. In the Community & Global Resilience in Energy Transitions (ENTR 190) course, MET students visit a local trail system to explore how regulation and land-use decisions shape energy systems and climate resilience on the ground. “The MET program reaffirmed that collaboration is key and people are key in the energy transition. Going into our careers, we will have to listen to all voices, loud and quiet, and incorporate those in a meaningful and respectful way to our solutions. People are the center of the energy issue and as long as we incorporate other people's perspectives in an equitable way, we will create energy outcomes that also promote societal good.” — Jordan Schisler, GR'26 Studying at the Irving Institute Situated between the Thayer School of Engineering and Tuck School of Business, with a direct view of the iconic Baker-Berry Library, the Institute serves as a hub of innovation, research, and collaboration. Our award-winning certified LEED Platinum facility was named 2024 Building of the Year by the New Hampshire Chapter of the U.S. Green Building Council (USGBC). The building was also awarded the prestigious American Institute of Architects (AIA) Committee on the Environment (COTE) 2025 Top Ten Award, recognizing sustainable design excellence. Inside, you'll find flexible classrooms, collaborative project spaces, and the inviting Fern Coffee and Tea Bar, ideal for a break between classes. MET students also have exclusive access to the Sandra L. Irving 1972a Commons, a full kitchen where they can store and prepare meals and drinks. Downstairs, a dedicated MET Lounge offers students their own space to relax and recharge. “Throughout the program, I worked on projects exploring affordable housing decarbonization, energy resilience in rural coastal communities across Maine, battery energy storage deployment, grid modernization, energy systems modeling, climate and energy data analytics, and campus decarbonization strategies. These experiences strengthened my understanding of how energy systems, policy, infrastructure, economics, and communities intersect, and reinforced my passion for developing solutions that are both technically effective and socially equitable.” Rebecca Middlen GR'26 Learning Outcomes Upon completing the program, you'll be prepared to collaborate with a wide range of stakeholders across the technical, economic, political, and social dimensions of energy systems and transitions. The MET program equips you with the skills, knowledge, and network to succeed in a rapidly evolving energy landscape. Program-Level Competencies Describe and analyze major dimensions of energy systems and transitions, including technological, business and financial, policy, and social dimensions. Develop and apply analytical frameworks and problem-solving skills to creatively address specific and systemic energy transition challenges. Contribute to, build, and lead multidisciplinary teams and partner effectively with diverse stakeholders. Assess the distribution of benefits and burdens in specific energy system contexts and propose actions that accelerate an affordable, reliable, equitable clean energy transition for all. Build skills necessary to thrive in current and future careers in the rapidly changing energy & climate industry. Connect with Us Ready to learn more? title: Mentorship, Networking & Community | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Mentorship, Networking & Community In Dartmouth's Master of Energy Transition (MET) program, you'll build meaningful personal connections while expanding your professional network — all with close support from the dedicated staff at the Irving Institute and Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies. Education Additional navigation Close Teaching and Learning at the Irving Institute Undergraduate Students Graduate Students Master of Energy Transition Degree Courses & Curriculum MET Faculty Mentorship, Networking & Community Career Treks Alumni & Careers Class of 2026 Profiles Class of 2027 Profiles Info Sessions & Admissions Events Apply to the MET Frequently Asked Questions Energy Justice Clinic Resources One-on-One Guidance & Countless Connections Professional Mentor Our Master of Energy Transition (MET) mentors are industry professionals from across the clean energy landscape, from corporate sustainability and finance to government, policy, and law; from engineering and manufacturing to entrepreneurship and consulting. Many mentors are Dartmouth alumni, some of whom are also members of the Irving Institute Advisory Board. Before you arrive on campus in September, you'll be thoughtfully matched with a mentor who aligns with your career interests and professional development goals. Throughout your studies, your mentor will offer one-on-one support and guidance. "The problems of today and the problems of tomorrow require a particularly holistic perspective. The MET program was created to deliver that: to create graduates who have the leadership skills to influence ideas, influence organizations, and influence sectors. Being a part of that is incredibly meaningful to me." — Daniel M. Kalafatas '96, Chairman and Co-Founder, 3Degrees; Irving Institute Advisory Board Member; and MET mentor Dedicated Career Coach As a MET student, you'll receive individualized support in navigating your professional path. Together with our MET Career Coach, you'll explore career options and connect your coursework, skills, and experiences with meaningful opportunities. From resume reviews and mock interviews to networking strategies and job search planning, your coach will be a consistent resource throughout your time in the program. Dartmouth Alumni Network The vibrant community of Dartmouth alumni extends around the world. Our alumni are actively engaged in the Irving Institute through the MET, our Advisory Board, special events, and more. As a student—and long after graduation—you'll find them to be welcoming, insightful, and eager to connect. Guest Speakers Each year, the Irving Institute hosts a wide range of events featuring guest speakers and panelists working at the forefront of energy, climate, and sustainability. MET students have special opportunities for small-group sessions with these experts, where you can ask questions, share perspectives, and build relationships with leaders across sectors. “I am especially grateful to the The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy and Society at Dartmouth Advisory Board members, whose guidance and experience have been a constant source of inspiration. Learning from professionals already working in the fields and sectors many of us aspire to join has been both motivating and grounding.” Fred Burondwa GR'26 Tight-Knit Cohort & Far-Reaching Support The MET Cohort Your MET cohort is small enough for genuine connection with peers and faculty. Because the program welcomes students from all academic backgrounds, you'll learn alongside classmates from fields as varied as the humanities, engineering, law, economics, and environmental and earth sciences. Some will have just finished their undergraduate degrees, some may be pursuing a second master's degree, and others will bring a few years of early-career experience. Together, you'll attend classes, workshops, and co-curricular events that sharpen your skills and deepen your learning. "Having people from an international perspective has really helped me, especially because the energy landscape is not just U.S.-dominated—it is a global field. So being able to work with people from around the world, get their perspectives and learn more about their ways of thinking has been really impactful for me." — Kadijat Alakiu GR'26, Energy Industry Analyst, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) MET students toured a Vermont-based solar and battery storage site as part of co-curricular programming, seeing firsthand the components that work together to create a reliable, renewable energy system. Fellow Dartmouth Graduate Students In addition to connecting with your MET cohort, you'll join the broader Dartmouth graduate student community. There are more than 2,000 graduate students at Dartmouth, with the majority obtaining degrees through the Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies. Because the MET is offered through the Guarini School, you will be included in events and gatherings around campus where you can connect with others living in the Hanover, NH area. The Institute's location on campus places you at the hub of interdisciplinary activity, with access to shared study spaces and cross-program collaboration. The Institute sits between the Thayer School of Engineering and Tuck School of Business, and MET students often connect with groups such as the Thayer Energy Club and the Tuck School's Revers Center for Energy, Sustainability and Innovation Fellows. Resources and Support The Master of Energy Transition is offered through Dartmouth's Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies and is administered by the Irving Institute. This unique partnership means you benefit from the full resources of both units, rooted in Dartmouth's 255-year tradition of academic excellence and impact. Guarini provides all of Dartmouth's 2000+ graduate students with robust academic, financial, and professional development support through its GuariniGRAD initiative. At the Irving Institute, you'll receive primary academic advising, along with personalized career development and community-building opportunities. “It’s exciting to have developed this cohort, and to know we all will be going out into this industry, and that our paths will continue to cross. The connections we’ve developed, both among ourselves and with alumni at Dartmouth, will continue to serve us. It’s exciting to think that all we’ve gained from the program isn’t over yet; it will continue.” Otto Schmidt GR'26, Associate, Energy and Environmental Economics (E3) Connect with Us Ready to learn more? title: Career Treks | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Career Treks One of the best ways to expand your network and define your career path is by making direct connections with professionals in the field. That's why we take Master of Energy Transition (MET) students on career treks to U.S. energy hubs, where you meet with decision-makers and staff, tour facilities, and hear directly from teams in industry, government, and local organizations about the current state of the energy sector. MET students talk with startup founders at the Greentown Labs Climatetech Summit. Education Additional navigation Close Teaching and Learning at the Irving Institute Undergraduate Students Graduate Students Master of Energy Transition Degree Courses & Curriculum MET Faculty Mentorship, Networking & Community Career Treks Alumni & Careers Class of 2026 Profiles Class of 2027 Profiles Info Sessions & Admissions Events Apply to the MET Frequently Asked Questions Energy Justice Clinic Resources A 360° view of the energy landscape You'll have the opportunity to take part in two career treks during your studies in the Master of Energy Transition (MET) program. Past treks have included trips to Boston, NYC, Houston, and the San Francisco Bay Area. The organizations we visit mirror the interdisciplinary MET curriculum, so you'll engage with sectors spanning technology, policy, finance, and community impact. Local trek hosts range in scale from early-stage startups to multinational energy companies, from municipal leaders to regional grid operators. We also often engage directly with Dartmouth alumni at host organizations and gatherings of local alumni clubs. Our past career treks have included visits with: Renewable energy and consulting firms A major utility and an independent grid operator—including a tour of their control room A sit-down lunch with state energy commissioners Cutting-edge research labs Grassroots climate advocacy coalitions Investment firms and meetings with venture investors Startup incubators and discussions with climatetech founders Offshore wind developers Geothermal developers AI-driven energy innovation platform developers “Learning directly from leaders in renewable energy, AI-driven energy innovation, consulting, and utility operations gave me a deeper understanding of the opportunities and challenges of the energy transition.” — Shariful Islam GR‘26, PhD student, University of Louisiana at Lafayette and researcher, Louisiana Solar Energy Lab What to expect on career treks The MET cohort travels together for 5-10 days, led by Irving Institute staff, meeting with teams at a wide range of organizations deeply involved in the clean energy transition. Every day begins with a briefing on the organizations you'll visit and the people you’ll meet. While each visit is different, they often include tours, meetings with staff, overviews of day-to-day operations, briefings from human resource professionals, testimonies from local community members, and personal career-path stories. Alongside downtime built into each trek, you'll also have dedicated time to set up meetings with new connections—a great way to learn more about potential professional opportunities. “The career treks connected academic concepts to real-life application, which is invaluable on its own, but even more importantly, we connected with alumni across the country in the energy sector. This made the community feel much larger than Hanover and reflects just how tight-knit and far-reaching the Dartmouth network truly is.” Amy Fulton GR'26 An extended classroom Career treks take classroom learning into the field, connecting you directly with the organizations shaping the energy transition. Beyond building your professional network, these immersive visits show how the many dimensions of socio-technical energy systems intersect in practice. For MET students, that may mean sitting down with global investors to explore how capital decisions balance risk, community impact, and long-term value. Or mapping the full energy value chain from trading to project development. Or examining how decades of experience in the oil and gas sector are informing the way emerging renewable technologies scale today. “On the California trek, I really felt an ‘aha’ moment, where I was able to see the implementation of all the things that we learned in courses in the field. So talking with Andrew McAllister '87, California Energy Commissioner, about how the California energy landscape looks, how the policy landscape looks, and things that they're dealing with, like high utility rates…. Those are all things we talked about in class, but seeing it firsthand from a commissioner's point of view was really impactful.” — Kadijat Alakiu GR'26, Energy Industry Analyst, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Frequently Asked Questions When are the career treks held? The Master of Energy Transition career treks take place when courses are not in session. The first trek is held in early December, between the fall term and winter term. The second trek is held in late March, during spring break. Are the treks required? Career treks are optional for Master of Energy Transition students. All students are eligible and encouraged to participate in at least one career trek during the program. Is there an additional cost for attending the career treks? Each Master of Energy Transition career trek requires a fee of $350. The fee contributes to the cost of travel, lodging, and most meals for the trek experience. Students may apply for financial aid if the career trek fee is a barrier to participation. This financial aid process would occur after the student is enrolled and is separate from the financial aid process for tuition. Who leads the career treks? Each career trek is led by Irving Institute staff, who manage the itinerary, travel, and hotel arrangements. Connect with Us Ready to learn more? title: Alumni & Careers | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Alumni & Careers The energy transition doesn't stay in one lane—and neither do MET graduates. Today's energy challenges demand professionals who can move fluidly across sectors and understand the diverse stakeholders shaping every project. The Dartmouth Master of Energy Transition prepares graduates to do exactly that. MET students meet with the senior partner and consultants at the Energy and Environmental Economics (E3) headquarters in San Francisco. Education Additional navigation Close Teaching and Learning at the Irving Institute Undergraduate Students Graduate Students Master of Energy Transition Degree Courses & Curriculum MET Faculty Mentorship, Networking & Community Career Treks Alumni & Careers Class of 2026 Profiles Class of 2027 Profiles Info Sessions & Admissions Events Apply to the MET Frequently Asked Questions Energy Justice Clinic Resources MET Alumni The Master of Energy Transition (MET) is designed to launch graduates into a broad range of meaningful careers. We welcome students from all academic backgrounds, and the paths our alumni take reflect that breadth—spanning the full range of organizations involved in the energy transition. The program is also an ideal complement to continued graduate study, including an MBA, PhD, or JD. MET alumni have gone on to roles in consulting, finance, analysis, and climate risk modeling, at organizations including a leading energy economics and strategic consulting firm, a renewable energy consulting firm, a major regional transmission organization, an independent transmission company, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC). Several have been accepted into distinguished law and doctoral programs where they continue their graduate studies. Kadijat Alakiu, GR'26 Energy Industry Analyst, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), Washington, D.C. “There’s a real focus on the career search. There’s even a joke about the 'fourth class,' which is our career search, networking, having coffee chats, interviewing. There’s a real emphasis on helping us get jobs. There are the career services, which have been extremely helpful. There’s our mentors, who have been vital to connecting us with people who either might be hiring or know someone who is hiring. So the professional development support has been beneficial.” Shariful Islam, GR'26 PhD student in Systems Engineering at Louisiana State University, Researcher at the Louisiana Solar Energy Lab “The MET program provided an exceptional interdisciplinary education, bringing together engineering, energy systems, economics, finance, policy, and leadership to prepare the next generation of energy leaders.” Riley Roach, GR'26 Commercial Analyst, Grid United, Houston “If we are to build a more reliable, affordable, and sustainable energy system, we must listen, engage, build trust, and keep people at the center of the conversation. While technology, policy, and markets are essential, meaningful progress ultimately depends on the communities and individuals these systems serve.” Otto Schmidt, GR'26 Associate, Energy and Environmental Economics, Inc. (E3), San Francisco “The energy industry is complex, with many different moving parts. There are different sectors within the energy industry, and different players. With regulation, there’s the mix of private and public sectors. That can be really difficult to get your hands around. And, as an undergraduate, I did not have classes that directly focused on that. So, the MET was a program that gave me a comprehensive picture of what the energy industry looks like, and made me feel confident that I can go into a room with an investment fund doing infrastructure work, or I can talk with someone who does policy in D.C., and I might not be the expert on that topic, but I can have a conversation about that and I understand where what they’re doing fits in with the larger context. For me, that’s extremely valuable.” Jordan Schisler, GR'26 Supply & Energy Management Rotational Analyst, Engie, Houston “The MET prepared me for what comes next through two aspects. One is through relevant energy experience that I can take into the field and leverage and learn. Then the other is professional experience. There's a lot of focus on how to network, how to build your network, how to talk with people. It's something that was invaluable to me in my career search. Those two aspects melded together is what made the MET really impactful for me.” Read more about the inaugural MET cohort: Browse Class of 2026 Profiles Career Trajectory As the global energy transition accelerates, organizations need problem-solvers and leaders who have a broad understanding of the full energy landscape. That's why the MET curriculum spans the full breadth of the energy sector: technology and science, law and policy, finance and economics, community and communications. Graduates are prepared for careers that shape how societies generate, distribute, and use energy—keeping equity, affordability, and reliability at the forefront. Energy job growth by the numbers Global renewable energy employment reached 16.6 million jobs in 2024 ( IRENA/ILO Renewable Energy and Jobs annual review ). In 2025, renewables surpassed coal in global power generation for the first time—accounting for 33.8% of global electricity—and solar alone met 75% of all new demand growth ( Ember, Global Electricity Review 2026 ). At the same time, AI infrastructure, data centers, and electrification are driving unprecedented power demand, while geopolitical conflicts repeatedly underscore supply chain fragility. Whether the motivation is cost, reliability, sustainability, or security, energy transition expertise has never been more essential. "Employers are desperately seeking graduates with capabilities in critical thinking. They want integrators - individuals who know how to connect the dots. To me, interdisciplinary training is not just the future of education, it's what top companies are looking for now. The MET program delivers on this need by weaving science, engineering, policy, and finance in a way that few programs around the world have managed to do." – Charlie Donovan, DBA, MET Faculty for ENTR 180, Finance & Accounting for the Energy Transition Energy professions and industries Roles the MET prepares you for: Analysis and assessment in energy, sustainability, markets, and risk Consulting in energy and climate strategy, sustainability, decarbonization, and energy economics Finance, investment, and economics project management Policy, regulatory and government affairs, permitting and compliance Program and project coordination/management for clean energy programs or grant administration Renewable and climate technology development and asset management Communications, public relations, and marketing specialists Areas the MET prepares you for: Corporate and industry: utilities, renewable energy developers, and oil & gas majors transitioning to clean energy Government, policy, and regulation, all at multiple levels of government Non-profit and community organizations Economics, finance, and investment Data analysis and modeling MET faculty member Cong Chen (left) joins MET students at CERAWeek 2026 in Houston—one of the world's foremost annual gatherings on energy, markets, and innovation, drawing more than 11,000 energy leaders from around the world. Scott Fisher “Dartmouth’s MET program trains students to identify, leverage, and integrate policy, business, and technology considerations in the context of the complexity of the energy sector — and develop innovative and comprehensive solutions.  This is critical to transform our energy systems. This approach also prepares the graduates to be nimble leaders, which is paramount because the energy landscape is constantly changing.” Scott G.
