I aim to apply this knowledge to accelerate the energy transition by modernizing conventional power systems through cleaner fuels, waste heat recovery, and integration of renewable technologies. Through Dartmouth's MET program, I hope to develop as a leader who can drive practical, scalable solutions for a sustainable energy future. Shariful's 2025 Bio Shariful Islam, a seasoned energy professional from Rajshahi, Bangladesh, specializes in power plant construction, operation, and management. With more than seven years of professional experience, Shariful has led the operation of a 226MW independent power plant at Confidence Power and Energy PLC., working with MAN 18V48/60TS engines and MARIM-4C2 turbines. His technical expertise covers Waste Heat Recovery Boilers (WHRB), Water Treatment Plants (WTP), Effluent Treatment Plants (ETP), Fuel Treatment Plants (FTP), HFO storage systems, and advanced control technologies. He is also an expert in operating DCS-Distributed Control System and SCADA-Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition systems for efficient and reliable plant performance. Shariful is committed to advancing the global energy transition, with expertise in sustainable sourcing, renewable energy integration, energy analysis and consulting, as well as smart grid and sustainable power solutions. Paul Kargol Current role: Contract Geologist, Big Rock Exploration, Charlottesville, Virginia Connect with Paul on LinkedIn Professional experience: Student Assistant, Washington and Lee University Researcher, Washington and Lee University Geographic Information System Intern, South Carolina Department of Natural Resources Undergraduate education: Geology BS, Washington & Lee, 2025 Paul's 2025 Bio Paul Kargol is pursuing a Master of Energy Transition at Dartmouth College, building upon his Bachelor of Science in Earth and Environmental Geosciences from Washington and Lee University. With expertise in GIS mapping, geophysical surveying, and environmental research, Paul has contributed to significant projects, including hydrostratigraphic research on the Ganges River delta aquifer system and coastal conservation initiatives with the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources. His technical proficiency spans ArcGIS Pro, RockWorks, and MATLAB, demonstrated through his work digitizing maps, conducting sediment analysis, and creating complex 3D geological models. Paul has presented his research at the national Geological Society of America conference and served as a founding member of his university's Sigma Gamma Epsilon chapter. Committed to sustainability and community engagement, Paul combines his scientific expertise with leadership experience and a passion for environmental stewardship, positioning him at the forefront of the energy transition field. Becca (Rebecca) Middlen Current program: JD student, Vermont Law and Graduate School Connect with Becca on LinkedIn Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program & how I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: I chose the Dartmouth Master of Energy Transition program because it combines technical expertise with policy and community engagement—an approach I believe is essential for equitable climate solutions. My background in environmental studies and coastal resilience research has shown me that science alone is not enough; law and policy must drive change. Through the MET, I aim to accelerate energy transitions by developing just and scalable strategies that center on vulnerable communities in the shift to net zero. Undergraduate education: Environmental Studies BA, Vassar College, 2025 Becca's 2025 Bio Rebecca Middlen is a recent graduate of Vassar College with a B.A. in Environmental Studies. Her undergraduate research examined how sea level rise reshapes coastal communities, but more broadly, she has pursued interdisciplinary approaches to environmental challenges—integrating ethical perspectives, historical context, and spatial analysis to advance net-zero objectives. Committed to environmental justice, Rebecca is particularly interested in how law can be leveraged to promote equitable responses to climate change. Following the completion of her Master's degree, she intends to enroll in law school and build a career in environmental policy, working to ensure that climate adaptation and mitigation strategies not only reduce emissions but also protect vulnerable communities and create more just environmental futures. Ella Reed Current role: Water Permitting Specialist, Oklahoma Public Water Resources Board, Oklahoma Connect with Ella on LinkedIn Professional experience: Teaching Assistant, Dartmouth College Research Assistant, University of Oklahoma Undergraduate education: Environmental Studies BA, Dartmouth, 2025 Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program & how I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: Dartmouth's Master of Energy Transition program represents the ideal next step in my journey towards becoming a leader in the environmental sector. The program's interdisciplinary curriculum, experiential learning opportunities, and focus on leadership development will provide me with the skills and knowledge necessary to drive meaningful change in the transition to sustainable energy systems. I am eager to immerse myself in the dynamic learning environment, collaborate with experts and peers, and apply my passion for clean energy to real world challenges. By pursuing this degree I am confident that I will be well-prepared to make a lasting impact on the global energy landscape and contribute to a more sustainable and equitable future for everyone. Ella's 2025 Bio With a strong academic background and a passion for interdisciplinary problem-solving, Ella focused much of her research on urban design and climate mitigation when working at the University of Oklahoma. She earned her BA from Dartmouth College in June 2025, majoring in Environmental Studies with a minor in Human-Centered Design. She is dedicated to developing innovative, practical solutions that drive sustainable and equitable transformations in urban environments. Riley Roach Current role: Commercial Analyst, Grid United, Houston, Texas Connect with Riley on LinkedIn Professional experience: Technical Summer Asset Analyst Intern, CleanCapital Operations Team Member, ASUREI, Appalachian State University Sales Representative, Mountain Running Company NSF I-Corps Research & Business Development Lead, National Science Foundation (NSF) Undergraduate education: Sustainable Technology BS, Appalachian State University, 2025 Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program & how I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: The Energy Trilemma – Energy Equality, Environmental Sustainable, and Energy Equity – is critical for a successful energy transition. The MET program implements these three pillars throughout each term. To be a catalyst in the energy transition, I must understand these three pillars, spread awareness; and, connect the dots between energy creation and energy access. Riley's 2025 Bio Riley Roach earned a Bachelor's degree in Sustainable Technology from Appalachian State University, complemented by minors in Entrepreneurial Studies and Community & Regional Planning. Riley was selected for the National Science Foundation Renewable Energy for Undergraduates (NSF REU) cohort, researching Resilient Carbon-Free U.S. Electric Power Systems. Her experience with the NSF I-Corps program led her to explore the commercial viability of algae as a biofuel. As a Technical Asset Management Intern at CleanCapital, Riley operated and maintained solar portfolios. As a recipient of the North Carolina Sustainable Energy Association Scholar Award, she engaged directly with clean energy stakeholders at the NCSEA conference. Beyond academics, Riley competed on the Women's Cross Country and Track team at Appalachian State, where she learned time management, teamwork, and accountability. Her career goal is to establish accessible, equitable, and reliable sustainable systems. Jordan Schisler Current role: Supply & Energy Management Rotational Analyst, ENGIE, Houston, Texas Connect with Jordan on LinkedIn Professional experience: Student Researcher in Heindel Lab, Kenyon College Philander Chase Conservancy Intern, Kenyon College Environmental Laboratory Teaching Assistant, Kenyon College Student Researcher, Boise State University Undergraduate education: Environmental Studies BA, Kenyon College, 2025 Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program & how I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: Renewable energy transitions are complex and require nuanced, interdisciplinary approaches to be both effective and equitable. I chose the MET program because of its comprehensive interdisciplinary training and the opportunity to collaborate with a diverse cohort of energy-focused scholars and professionals. I am committed to advancing energy transitions through my passion for conducting community-engaged research and developing effective, compassionate ways to communicate scientific findings with both the local community and industry stakeholders Jordan's 2025 Bio Jordan has extensive research experience across diverse labs and projects, along with strong skills in communicating research, supported by a background in teaching and curating science education content. With this expertise, Jordan brings a passion for interdisciplinary research collaboration and advancing effective science communication. At Dartmouth, she continues to deepen my understanding of the multifaceted challenges and opportunities in advancing renewable energy by integrating her enthusiasm for climate science, energy research, and community involvement. She is actively pursuing researcher or research analyst positions where she can apply her skills in communication, critical thinking, and data analysis to accelerate the transition to clean energy. Otto Schmidt Current role: Associate, E3 - Energy and Environmental Economics, Inc., San Francisco, California Connect with Otto on LinkedIn Professional experience: Physics Laboratory Teaching Assistant, St. Olaf College Consultant and Research Fellow: Center for Interdisciplinary Research, St. Olaf College Undergraduate Researcher - Impacts of Snow Evolution Research Lab, St. Olaf College Consulting Engineers Group Inc (CEG): Engineering Intern Apogee Adventures, Outdoor Trip Leader Undergraduate education: Physics and Mathematics BS, St Olaf's College, 2025 Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program & how I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: I chose the Master of Energy Transition program because of its cross-disciplinary coursework and the varied backgrounds of its tight-knit cohort. I intend to use my ability to work across industries and expertise areas to bring organizations forward with analytically supported and people-centered solutions. I believe community is essential for driving the energy transition forward Otto's 2025 Bio Otto Schmidt earned a dual B.A. in Physics and Mathematics with a focus in Statistics and Data Science from St. Olaf College. At St. Olaf, Otto conducted research on snow albedo, worked as a statistical consultant for biology faculty, captained the cross country and track teams, and studied in Ecuador, Jordan, Namibia, and Vietnam. He interned with Consulting Engineers Group, where he developed an energy market price prediction tool for battery owners. Otto's array of experiences guides his interdisciplinary thinking and communication. Otto's leadership skills are bolstered by guiding backpacking trips for young adults in Europe, Canada, and the US. Through this, he instills confidence, community, and passion for the outdoors in the next generation. He is currently pursuing a Master of Energy Transition at Dartmouth. Strong communication supports his goal of advising businesses and governments to take impactful steps toward sustainability as they navigate a shifting energy landscape. Matteo Tafuri Professional experience: Research Project on Infrastructure Economics & Project Finance, Bocconi University Corporate Financial Planning & Analysis (FP&A) Intern - Energy & Infrastructure Group, Maire Tecnimont Group S.p.A. Strategy & Investment Analyst, Independent Real Assets Initiative Early Career Program Trainee with Intesa Sanpaolo Bank - Banking & Venture Capital, Zest Group (formerly LVenture Group Connect with Matteo on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Economics & Business Administration BSc, Bocconi University (Milan, Italy), 2024 Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program & how I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: I chose Dartmouth's MET program because it uniquely combines engineering depth with business and finance expertise in the energy & infrastructure industry. For someone pursuing a career in energy and infrastructure finance, this integration is essential: technology without financial structuring cannot scale, and finance without technical insight cannot deliver impact.  I am to apply my skills in project finance, infrastructure investment, and transaction strategy to advance the evolution of energy & infrastructure systems in global markets. Matteo's 2025 Bio Matteo holds a BSc in Economics and Business Administration from Bocconi University, where he completed his thesis on financing frameworks for large-scaleinfrastructure through Public-Private Partnerships (PPP's). At Maire Tecnimont Group, a listed energy & infrastructure engineering group, he worked on corporate financial analysis, performing due diligence, contractor risk assessments, and financial evaluations across North America, EMEA and Asia. His academic training built a strong foundation in project finance and PPP structuring, while his experience as a Strategy & Investment Analyst at an independent real assets venture provided exposure to development strategy and portfolio asset management. Fluent in Italian and English, and conversational in Chinese and Spanish, Matteo is originally from Rome, Italy. Outside of his academic and professional interests, he enjoys playing soccer, tennis, and sailing. Krutika Umashankar Current role: Market Risk Analyst, BP, Chicago, Illinois Connect with Krutika on LinkedIn Professional experience: Analyst (Coffee), Ofi Data Analyst, Olam Transfer Pricing Associate, IC Advisors Research Assistant, Centennial Asia Advisors Undergraduate education: Economics - Political Science & International Relations BA, Cardiff University (Wales), 2017 Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program & how I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: I chose Dartmouth's MET program for its strategic location and powerful network in commodities trading, which will be essential for my career pivot from soft commodities to energy markets. The program allows me to combine my analytical expertise with energy transition knowledge, positioning me to accelerate transitions as a commodity analyst. I'll apply rigorous data analysis and forecasting to energy trading, helping capital flow toward cleaner sources while navigating this market transformation. Krutika's 2025 Bio Krutika is a commodities analyst with six years of experience in soft commodities markets. She specializes in leveraging data analysis, scenario modeling, and forecasting to support strategic decision-making. Her expertise lies in synthesizing diverse data sources, from trade flows to weather patterns in major cocoa and coffee growing regions. She translates these insights into actionable strategies for trading teams. Throughout her career, Krutika has partnered with sales and trading desks to generate profitable trade ideas and sharpen forecasts, combining quantitative rigor with seasoned market instincts. Currently, she is pursuing a Master of Energy Transition at Dartmouth College to broaden my expertise from soft commodities into renewable energy markets and transition economics. This progression is a deliberate step to align her analytical background and experience in environmental supply chains with the rapidly changing demands of the energy sector. Krutika aims to leverage her expertise across the evolving energy and commodity markets. Chloe (Run) Yang Current program: PhD student at Colorado State University Connect with Chloe on LinkedIn Professional experience: Energy Data & Digitalization Analyst Intern, China Huaneng Group Green Finance Analyst Intern, Ping An Bank Co., Ltd Data Analyst Intern, Yunnan KunJiaoTou Supply Chain Co., Ltd. Backend Engineer Intern, Juxiang Technology Co., Ltd. Conducted research on Large Language Models (LLMs), Research Assistant, Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, University of Nottingham (China) Undergraduate education: Computer Science BS, University of Nottingham (China), 2025 Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program & how I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: My internships in energy and finance showed me how technology can transform these sectors, while my AI research revealed the potential of advanced algorithms for complex optimization. However, technical skills alone aren't enough: Dartmouth's MET program provides the interdisciplinary foundation I need to bridge computer science with energy systems and policy. I intend to accelerate the energy transition by developing AI-driven tools for grid optimization and renewable integration, making clean energy more efficient and reliable while ensuring these solutions are practical and deployable in real-world systems. Chloe's 2025 Bio Chloe studied computer science at the University of Nottingham, but discovered she is more passionate about using technology to tackle real environmental challenges. At China Huaneng Group, she worked on data integration systems for hydropower operations and energy digitalization, while her experience at Ping An Bank exposed her to green finance and ESG frameworks driving sustainable investments. Her undergraduate research on Large Language Models now informs her current work on LLM-based approaches for electrical grid stability and renewable energy integration. She applies machine learning and Python-based data analysis to energy challenges like demand forecasting, grid optimization, and fault detection. Chloe has competed in mathematical modeling competitions and is passionate about bridging AI capabilities with practical energy transition needs. Outside of work, Chloe stays active with piano, tennis, and boxing. Now she is looking to combine her background with a growing interest in sustainability, with the goal of using data and technology to make a meaningful contribution to the energy transition.

text: Class of 2027 Profiles Education Additional navigation Close Teaching and Learning at the Irving Institute Undergraduate Students Graduate Students Master of Energy Transition Degree Courses & Curriculum MET Faculty Mentorship, Networking & Community Career Treks Alumni & Careers Class of 2026 Profiles Class of 2027 Profiles Info Sessions & Admissions Events Apply to the MET Frequently Asked Questions Energy Justice Clinic Resources Meet the Class of 2027 Coming from fields as varied as economics, environmental science, international relations, and engineering, Master of Energy Transition students share a drive to build practical solutions, lead with confidence, and move the energy transition forward. Justus J Dubois Connect with Justus on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Environmental Studies BA, Dartmouth College, 2026 Bio: JJ Dubois graduated from Dartmouth College in 2026 with a B.A. in Environmental Studies and is interested in pursuing a career in energy consulting. During his time at Dartmouth, he was a member of the men’s rowing team, an experience that strengthened his work ethic, discipline, and ability to perform as part of a team. Outside of academics and professional interests, he enjoys spending as much time outdoors as possible and is always keen to try different sports and activities. He is particularly passionate about surfing and sailing and enjoys being around the ocean. Looking ahead, JJ hopes to combine his interest in energy and sustainability with his analytical and collaborative skills to contribute to the ongoing energy transition. Hannah Garrou Connect with Hannah on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Economics BA, Swarthmore College, 2026 Professional experience: Needham & Co., Investment Banking Intern Ara Partners, Private Equity Intern Fayez Sarofim & Co., Investment Intern Why I chose Dartmouth’s MET program: I chose Dartmouth’s MET program to build on my background in economics and finance while developing a deeper understanding of the technologies, markets, and policies shaping the energy transition. I was especially drawn to the program’s interdisciplinary approach and its connection to industry. I hope to use the MET experience to prepare for a career at the intersection of energy, economics, and investment. Bio: Hannah Garrou graduated from Swarthmore College in 2026 with a B.A. in Economics, where she also competed on the varsity track and field team and served as a team captain. Her professional experience includes private equity at Ara Partners, where she researched investment opportunities related to industrial decarbonization, and public equity investing at Fayez Sarofim & Co. These experiences sparked her interest in how capital, markets, and technology can shape the energy transition. At Dartmouth, Hannah is building a deeper technical and industry understanding of the energy system while continuing to explore the economic and investment questions surrounding its transition. She hopes to pursue a career in the energy industry following the MET program. Tyler Haas Connect with Tyler on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Environmental Science BA, Franklin & Marshall College, 2016 Professional experience: Energy Consultant, Tesla Associate Vice President, Compliance, OTC Markets Group Project Manager, Lightbox Energy Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program: I choose the Master of Energy Transition program at Dartmouth because of the people. Before joining the program, I was able to speak with a handful of students, professors, and Irving Institute Staff. A common theme between all of them was a desire to accelerate the Energy Transition, and a willingness to answer questions. Bio: In the past decade Tyler has worked in renewable energy, financial compliance, and sustainable infrastructure operations. A graduate of Franklin & Marshall College with a degree in Environmental Science, his experience includes siting solar energy projects, analyzing financial markets, and managing projects for a sustainable infrastructure deployment firm. He has also collaborated closely with local governments to implement sustainability initiatives. Tyler brings an interdisciplinary perspective to the challenges of clean energy deployment. Through the Master of Energy Transition program, he seeks to integrate these experiences, strengthen his ability to move projects from ambition to implementation, and support a more sustainable, and resilient, energy future for all. Muhammad Hashim Khan Connect with Muhammad on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Economics BS, National University of Sciences and Technology, 2026 Professional experience: Founder and Owner, Tajjal Olive Pakistan Finance Intern, A.F. Ferguson and Co. (PwC Network) Finance Intern, Gigi Industries Limited Finance Intern, Pearl Continental Hotel How I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: I intend to accelerate the energy transition by helping direct capital toward renewable energy infrastructure in markets that global finance has yet to fully reach. Pakistan's energy crisis is not abstract to me, having lived through it. My goal is to work in energy project finance, structuring the deals that get clean energy built in emerging markets where the need is urgent and the gap between ambition and investment is widest. Bio: Hashim is originally from Rawalpindi, Pakistan. He holds a Bachelor of Science in Economics from the National University of Sciences and Technology, where he conducted  research applying macroeconomic modeling to Pakistani fiscal and monetary policy in order to predict consumption and investment behavior and drive policy. Prior to Dartmouth, he launched Tajjal Olive, a fully sustainable, solar-powered commercial business producing premium extra virgin olive oil, representing a complete transition from conventional energy sources such as diesel to renewable infrastructure. He has also completed internships in the finance sector at A.F. Ferguson and Co. (PwC Network) and other firms in Pakistan. Hashim’s primary career aim is energy project finance in the United States, where he intends to develop the expertise, networks and technical acumen to eventually bring those capabilities back to emerging markets such as South Asia and help drive the clean energy transition where it is most desperately needed. Evan Kurash Connect with Evan on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Economics BA & Environmental Studies BA, St. Lawrence University, 2026 Professional experience: 7 years in residential construction 2025 internship digitizing an inventory system for ATPackaging Outlier AI, training and developing LLM Bio: As a resident of Vermont, Evan grew up with a strong connection to and enjoyment of nature and its preservation. This sparked his passion for the integration of renewable and carbon free energy forms to help preserve the environment that he grew up loving. Attending Dartmouth in the MET program is perfect step to help Evan acquire the skills and knowledge needed to help accelerate the transition to a more sustainable level. Elaine Li Undergraduate education: Economics BA & Environmental Studies BA, Dartmouth College, 2026 Tokelo Makepe Connect with TK on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Business (Economic Consulting) BS, Kelley School of Business, Indiana University, 2026 Professional experience: Investment Analyst Intern, Listed Equities, Botswana Insurance Fund Management (BIFM) President, 180 Degrees Consulting, Indiana University Bio: Tokelo "TK" Makepe, from Gaborone, Botswana, is a Master of Energy Transition student at Dartmouth. He graduated from Indiana University's Kelley School of Business with a degree in Economic Consulting, studying as a Government of Botswana Top Achievers Scholar, selected from roughly 50,000 applicants. At Indiana University, he served as president of 180 Degrees Consulting, leading pro bono engagements for nonprofits, which was his first professional introduction to work in the energy sector. He working specifically with a renewable energy company based out of sub-Saharan Africa. Most recently, TK was an Investment Analyst on a Listed Equities team, where he supported public-equity research and investment analysis, working across a number of industries with a particular focus on downstream energy firms. Gordie Means Connect with Gordie on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Renewable Energy  B.Tech., SUNY Morrisville, 2026 Professional experience: Project Manager, Nickels Energy Solutions, Liverpool, NY How I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: I intend to accelerate the energy transition by closing the gap between clean-energy projects and the grid that must absorb them. After leading roughly 75 residential solar installations, I have seen how distributed renewables are reshaping the grid. I will combine my Renewable Energy degree, field experience, and Dartmouth's MET program to deploy renewables, battery storage, inverter-based resources, and virtual power plants that connect faster, operate flexibly, and deliver reliable, affordable clean power. Bio: Gordie Means is a Renewable Energy graduate of SUNY Morrisville, where he earned a B.Tech. magna cum laude. As a Project Manager at Nickels Energy Solutions, he has led approximately 75 residential solar PV installations of up to 25 kW, supervised crews of up to seven installers, and trained seven new team members. A self-taught mechanic, he has rebuilt engines and vehicle electrical systems, and he served on SUNY Morrisville's Sustainability Council, helping the college earn a STARS Silver rating. Gordie's interests center on battery energy storage, inverter-based resources, interconnection, and virtual power plants. He is pursuing solar and storage project delivery, development, or grid services roles in the Northeast. Nicholas Nassuphis Connect with Nicholas on LinkedIn Prior g raduate education: Master of Arts (Triple Honours), International Relations with Modern Languages (French and German), University of St Andrews, 2026 Professional experience: Renewable Energy Private Equity Intern, True Green Capital Management Treasury Intern – Integrated Oil & Gas, VARO Energy Energy & Resources Consulting Intern, Baringa Partners Investigative Consulting Intern, G3 Good Governance Group Debt Servicing Intern, RoundShield Partners Why I chose Dartmouth’s MET program: I chose Dartmouth’s MET program because it uniquely combines technology, business, economics, finance and policy, reflecting the interdisciplinary nature of the energy transition. My experiences showed me that successful transitions require balancing sustainability, affordability and energy security, and that doing so requires both technical understanding and commercial expertise. Having experienced Dartmouth through the Tuck Business Bridge Program, I was eager to return to its collaborative environment and gain the multidisciplinary skills needed for a career in energy investment and transactions. Bio: Nicholas holds a Master of Arts (Triple Honours) in International Relations with Modern Languages (French and German) from the University of St Andrews, where his academic work explored energy policy and geopolitics. At True Green Capital, a renewable energy private equity firm, he worked on investment origination and acquisition opportunities. At VARO Energy, an integrated oil and gas company, he supported the development of derivative structures for purchasing ETS2 carbon emissions certificates. At Baringa, he supported retail strategy and transformation for the UK’s largest legacy energy retailer, including work on innovative electricity tariffs. These experiences strengthened his ambition to pursue an energy-focused M&A advisory role in New York. Fluent in English, French, German and Greek, Nicholas has a British, German and Greek background. Outside of his academic and professional interests, he enjoys tennis, golf, windsurfing and scuba diving. Emme Nelson Connect with Emme on LinkedIn Prior graduate education: Management and Sustainable Development, University of St Andrews, 2026 Professional experience: University of St Andrews: Undergraduate Research, Sustainable Development & Energy Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program: I chose Dartmouth’s Master of Energy Transition because its interdisciplinary approach reflects the complexity of today’s energy challenges. The MET program’s emphasis on systems thinking, energy justice, policy, finance, and real-world application directly aligns with my interests and future goals. I was drawn to Dartmouth’s collaborative environment, small classes, and access to faculty actively engaged in energy research. The MET program will expand my analytical and leadership capabilities and prepare me to bridge industry realities with sustainability while notably contributing to meaningful, equitable energy solutions. Bio: Emelie (Emme) Nelson is from Fort Worth, Texas, where energy was never an abstract concept. Energy shaped communities, careers, conversations, and the world around her. She earned an Upper Second-Class Master of Arts (Honours) degree in Management and Sustainable Development from the University of St Andrews in Scotland. Moving from Texas to Scotland broadened her perspective and gave her the opportunity for cultural immersion and opportunities to readily explore different countries, environments, and landscapes. Throughout her undergraduate studies, Emme explored the relationship between energy, human behavior, sustainability, and society. These explorations including research involving Indigenous communities in North and South America, a topic particularly meaningful because of her family’s Native American heritage. Her experiences taught her the importance of understanding issues from multiple perspectives and how meaningful environmental changes begin at the individual, community, and governance levels. Now at Dartmouth, she combines her Texas roots, international experiences, inquisitive nature, and commitment to learning as she continues to concentrate on the ever-evolving energy landscape. Stella Odoyo Connect with Stella on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Bioenvironmental Engineering BS & Accounting (Supply Chain Management) BS, Rutgers University, 2016 Professional experience: Copenhagen Offshore Partners Suffolk Construction JPMorgan Chase Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program: I chose Dartmouth's MET program because I wanted the technical and policy depth the program provides to match my finance operational experience in offshore wind — and to sharpen my ability to lead strategic capital and infrastructure decisions in the energy transition. Dartmouth's interdisciplinary approach lets me pair my  finance background with a rigorous, systems-level understanding of the energy transition. Bio: Stella Odoyo is a Finance Business Partner professional with a career spanning offshore wind energy, construction, and financial services. She holds dual Bachelor of Science degrees in Bioenvironmental Engineering and Accounting, with a concentration in supply chain management, from Rutgers University (2016). Her professional experience includes Copenhagen Offshore Partners, Suffolk Construction, and JPMorgan Chase, where she led financial analysis, forecasting, budgeting, and P&L management across large-scale infrastructure and investment portfolios. In the Master of Energy Transition program at Dartmouth College, she is deepening her technical and strategic expertise in the energy transition. She is driven by a commitment to leading strategic projects that advance the energy transition. Molly Smith Connect with Molly on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Environmental Studies BA, College of the Holy Cross, 2026 Professional experience: Office Engineer Co-op, United Civil - GCEP How I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: Accelerating the energy transition depends not only on clean technology, but also on the organizations that have to adopt it. That takes people who can connect innovation, policy, and industry, and who are prepared to lead. I intend to contribute by working where those areas meet, helping organizations, including companies working to decarbonize, turn ambitious goals into practical, measurable progress. Dartmouth's Master of Energy Transition gives me the interdisciplinary experience and the network to succeed in this field, along with experiential learning to address real-world challenges. My ultimate goal is to help build a cleaner, more resilient, and more just energy system. Bio: Molly Smith earned a B.A. in Environmental Studies from the College of the Holy Cross, where she developed an interdisciplinary perspective on environmental challenges and their impacts on people, communities, and society. Her studies shaped her belief that effective climate solutions must address both environmental outcomes and the social realities of the energy transition. Molly is particularly interested in corporate sustainability and decarbonization, with a focus on helping high-emitting companies reduce their environmental impact and take greater accountability for their contributions to climate change. She hopes to help build a more just and equitable energy system where the benefits and burdens of the transition are fairly distributed. Her experience with GIS mapping and Excel has strengthened her ability to analyze and communicate environmental information, while her interdisciplinary background has taught her to approach complex challenges from multiple perspectives. At Dartmouth, she hopes to build the technical and practical knowledge needed to advance meaningful corporate climate action. Blair Tran Connect with Blair on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Economics BA, Soka University of America, 2026 Professional experience: BrightNight Power, Energy Analyst Intern Boundless Impact Research & Analytics, Renewables Analyst Intern Energy Innovation Capital, Investment Intern United Nations Development Program (UNDP) Vietnam, Energy Transition Intern Youth4Climate Policy Working Group How I intend to help accelerate the energy transition: I’m drawn to the commercial side of the energy transition, where market dynamics and project economics shape which projects move forward. I want to leverage energy market insights to structure supply contracts, offtake agreements, and business strategies for utility-scale renewables, helping developers manage risk and secure financing. After the MET program, I plan to build a career across power markets, origination, and commercial strategy, helping bring innovative power solutions to market. Bio: Blair’s interest in the power sector began with experiencing firsthand how energy access and infrastructure reliability shape everyday life in Vietnam. A recent graduate of Soka University of America studying Economics and Social Behavioral Science, she has built experiences across electricity market analytics, commercial strategy, low-carbon technology research, and climate policy. Previously at BrightNight Power, she supported PPA origination by analyzing power and gas markets and offtake structures across a 30 GW solar and storage portfolio. At Boundless Impact, she conducted lifecycle and techno-economic analyses for investors evaluating vehicle-to-grid and geothermal technologies. Before college, Blair spent a gap year traveling across the Mekong Delta while supporting UNDP Vietnam in launching its first youth-led climate education initiative and policy advocacy campaign ahead of COP26. She plans to build a career in energy strategy and analytics, applying market insights to the development and financing of clean energy infrastructure. Christopher Ward Connect with Christopher on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Environmental Policy and Economics, Colby College, 2024 Bio: Chris went to Colby college where he studied environmental policy and economics and graduated in 2024. He has worked with the Phippsburg, Maine Comprehensive Plan Committee, helping develop risk assessments for natural resources and developing GIS maps for critical infrastructure. Prior to that he helped the Lyttelton, New Zealand local government with climate risk assessments to predict vulnerable areas of sedimentation for their harbor. Following the MET, Chris plans to begin a career either in green energy project finance or join an emerging energy technology startup. When Chris isn’t contemplating energy transitions he enjoys playing chess and hiking. Jack Whiting Connect with Jack on LinkedIn Undergraduate education: Mathematics & Economics BA, Bowdoin College, 2019 Professional experience: Team Lead, Avalanche Route Leader and Trail Crew Member, Park City Ski Patrol Systems Operations Associate, Collective Health Researcher & Writer, The Bowdoin Review Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program: I chose the MET because the interdisciplinary curriculum and faculty offer an opportunity to develop a systems-level view of the energy system. I believe that renewable energy technologies offer an opportunity to create a future that is not only sustainable, but also materially abundant and supportive of just societies. To contribute to such a future, an understanding of the technological, economic, and social dimensions of energy is essential. The incredibly committed network of Dartmouth alumni is also a nice bonus! Bio: Jack earned a dual B.A. in Math and Economics from Bowdoin College, where he played defensive back on the football team and wrote for The Bowdoin Review. After graduating, he moved to Salt Lake City to build data tools for Collective Health, a rapidly-growing tech company. His desk at CH offered a spectacular view of the Wasatch Mountains, and after three years of looking at them, he took a chance and joined the Park City Ski Patrol. Over five years of full-time patrolling, Jack grew into a leadership role coordinating alpine emergency response teams, leading crack-of-dawn avalanche control routes, and connecting with the natural world. Witnessing the Wasatch's dwindling snowpack up close left a lasting impression on Jack and motivates his current work as an MET student. Jack hopes to use the leadership, communication and quantitative skills he developed in earlier roles to contribute to electricity sector decarbonization. Bin (Benjamin) Wu Undergraduate education: University College London, 2025, Bachelor of Science in Statistics with Economics and Finance Professional experience: Renewable Energy / Corporate Strategy & Quantitative Analysis Intern, Jinko Solar Merger & Acquisition Intern, AIG Investments, LLC Corporate Strategy Intern, Fosun Group Why I chose Dartmouth's MET program: I chose Dartmouth’s Master of Energy Transition program to bridge quantitative financial rigor with scalable clean-tech solutions. Having analyzed solar photovoltaic supply chains at Jinko Solar and tackled land degradation through my environmental NGO in Inner Mongolia, I wanted an interdisciplinary engineering framework. Dartmouth’s systems-level approach uniquely equips me to finance and deploy decentralized renewable grids, accelerating the global shift toward a low-carbon economy. Bio: Bin (Benjamin) Wu holds a B.S. in Statistics with Economics and Finance from University College London. Blending quantitative financial modeling with a deep passion for sustainability, Bin has built diverse professional experience across M&A at AIG Investments, corporate strategy at Fosun Group and TikTok, and renewable energy research at Jinko Solar. Beyond corporate finance, Bin is deeply committed to grassroots environmental action. As the founder of an Inner Mongolia-based ecological association, he led teams to raise funding, partner with government bureaus, and combat desertification.  Bin aims to leverage his technical and financial background to accelerate global clean energy infrastructure development and market-driven climate solutions. title: Frequently Asked Questions | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Frequently Asked Questions In Dartmouth's nine-month Master of Energy Transition (MET) degree program, you’ll build expertise in the technologies, economics, and policies driving the global shift toward clean energy. Engaging with our active alumni network and your MET student cohort, you’ll be immersed in a community that is dedicated to decarbonization and equity at local and global levels. Our interdisciplinary, project-rich curriculum prepares you with real-world skills needed to help power a more sustainable, climate-stable future. Education Additional navigation Close Teaching and Learning at the Irving Institute Undergraduate Students Graduate Students Master of Energy Transition Degree Courses & Curriculum MET Faculty Mentorship, Networking & Community Career Treks Alumni & Careers Class of 2026 Profiles Class of 2027 Profiles Info Sessions & Admissions Events Apply to the MET Frequently Asked Questions Energy Justice Clinic Resources About the Degree What kind of degree is the Master of Energy Transition (MET)? The Master of Energy Transition (MET) is a professional degree program. While you will get hands-on experience working on real-world problems through individual courses, you will not conduct a major independent research project or thesis. Can the MET be combined with any other Dartmouth degrees? There are currently no formal joint degree programs with the MET. However, as an accelerated, professional degree program, the MET is an ideal complement to other Dartmouth graduate degrees, such as the MBA, Master of Engineering, or Master of Engineering Management. Admissions Where can I learn more about the application and admission process? The Master of Energy Transition is a program in Dartmouth's Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies . Review the Master of Energy Transition admission requirements . Review additional admissions information for the Guarini School of Graduate and Advanced Studies . Visit Guarini Admissions Frequently Asked Questions . Can my credentials be evaluated before I apply? Dartmouth application reviewers consider all components of an application. It is not possible to provide assessments before a complete application has been submitted. Is there an enrollment deposit? ​​​​​​A non-refundable $500 enrollment deposit is required upon acceptance of an admission offer. Are there any coursework or job-related prerequisites? Academic or job experience in energy is not required. The Master of Energy Transition is designed for a wide range of learners from diverse backgrounds and disciplines who are driven to help society accelerate energy transitions and address climate change in their careers. If you do not have a STEM background, you will have opportunities to develop and enhance your quantitative skills. Can I use AI to complete my application? We read and evaluate your application to the MET program to learn about you, your experiences, and what you hope the MET will enable you to do. You know yourself much better than AI does. So, we encourage you to write about your experiences and how the MET will enhance your professional and personal development. Is the program open to international students, and are graduates eligible for STEM-OPT? Yes, we encourage international students to apply for the Master of Energy Transition. The Master of Energy Transition is a STEM-designated program, and international graduates are eligible to apply for STEM-OPT . Do I have to submit English Language Proficiency scores for admission to the MET? Language proficiency test scores are required for non-US citizens, with the exception of those who will have graduated with a bachelor's (or higher) degree after having studied for at least four years at an institution in the U.S. or Canada. We accept TOEFL, IELTS, and Duolingo. Financial Aid Is financial aid available? Yes, the Irving Institute offers a limited number of need-based, partial tuition scholarships that can cover up to 60% of your tuition. These unique scholarships are available only to Master of Energy Transition (MET) students. The Irving Institute also offers a limited number of merit scholarships. No additional application is required to be considered. Your admissions application will be reviewed upon submission for a merit scholarship. Learn more about MET scholarships . Learn more about financial aid for graduate students . Can international students apply for financial aid? Yes. International students can apply for a need-based Master of Energy Transition (MET) scholarship . There are options for additional financial support for international students as well. For example, there are student employment opportunities , and international students may be eligible for certain private loans . You can contact the Dartmouth Financial Aid office for more information about loans for international students. Courses & Curriculum Who are the instructors? A talented group of Dartmouth professors, lecturers, and expert practitioner-instructors teach our courses, ensuring you are immersed in a broad range of academic and professional perspectives and expertise. Meet the MET faculty . Do Master of Energy Transition (MET) students conduct research? The MET is a professional degree program and emphasizes real-world experience through project-based courses. There are no formal research or thesis components or requirements. Is there an internship requirement? The Master of Energy Transition program does not require a formal internship. Instead, experiential learning is interwoven throughout the curriculum . Our project-based courses serve as mini-internships — allowing you to gain hands-on experience with real-world challenges through our partner organizations. This is one of many opportunities to build your skills and professional network. If you are seeking a formal internship outside of the program, you'll find that the schedule of the program allows for a summer internship prior to the program start or following graduation. Careers & Mentorship What are the mentorship and industry experience opportunities? Expert mentorship and real-world experience are built into the core of the Master of Energy Transition program. Mentorship: When you begin the program, you'll be thoughtfully paired with a mentor from our vast community of Dartmouth alumni energy and climate leaders. Mentors will provide support throughout the program, including personalized career advice and networking opportunities. Projects: You'll complete several project-based courses, enabling you to gain real-world experience. Through our partnerships with leading industries and organizations, we offer highly relevant and timely hands-on projects and data sets. Master of Energy Transition Faculty Director, Professor Geoff Parker , holds more than a decade of experience building and teaching highly impactful industry-engaged project courses. What career resources and support are available for Master of Energy Transition students? You’ll benefit from personalized career mentorship and support, along with opportunities for professional development, including career treks where you’ll meet industry leaders as well as career panels featuring a diverse range of professionals. Our dedicated program staff, faculty, and engaged alumni network offer timely insight into the skills and experience that today’s employers value across business, non-profit, and government sectors. Additionally, GuariniGRAD offers Career Development resources and guidance . What types of jobs are graduates prepared for? The Master of Energy Transition equips students with multidisciplinary knowledge and skills essential for a wide range of positions in energy, climate, sustainability, and adjacent fields. Potential roles include: Energy and/or climate analyst Consulting and coordinating roles in business, policy, and sustainability Project and program management and leadership roles for corporate, government, and non-profit entities Communications and engagement positions View more energy sector career information . Student Life Where can I learn more about being a graduate student at Dartmouth? Dartmouth offers comprehensive graduate student support in academics, career development, community, professional development, and wellness. Visit the GuariniGRAD site to learn more . As an education program at Dartmouth College, the Clinic provides applied social science collaborations with community partners working toward horizontal learning relationships. title: Courses & Curriculum | The Arthur L. Irving Institute for Energy & Society
text: Courses & Curriculum Dartmouth's Master of Energy Transition (MET) curriculum is grounded in interdisciplinary learning, with a consistent emphasis on the energy transition's impact on social systems and community well-being, locally and globally. MET faculty member Cong Chen, Assistant Professor of Engineering, teaches Data Analytics for Energy and Climate (ENTR 140). Education Additional navigation Close Teaching and Learning at the Irving Institute Undergraduate Students Graduate Students Master of Energy Transition Degree Courses & Curriculum MET Faculty Mentorship, Networking & Community Career Treks Alumni & Careers Class of 2026 Profiles Class of 2027 Profiles Info Sessions & Admissions Events Apply to the MET Frequently Asked Questions Energy Justice Clinic Resources Cultivating a Community of Energy Leaders Dartmouth's non-thesis, professional Master of Energy Transition (MET) program prepares you to make an immediate impact in the clean energy transition. With in-person courses on Dartmouth's scenic campus, you'll benefit from meaningful connections with instructors, fellow students, guest speakers, and industry and nonprofit partners, all in a collaborative academic setting. "Our energy systems are the backbone of modern life, and they are under extreme pressure to transform. The challenges this creates do not respect borders of any kind — disciplinary, national, or geographic. It has been a dream to build a program that is laser-focused on increasing society's capacity to not just address these challenges, but to use them as an opportunity to build a better world." — Amanda Graham, PhD, Director of Academic Programs & the MET Course Descriptions The MET program spans three academic terms. During each 10-week term, you'll complete three courses. Our courses are organized into three thematic areas. Technology of Energy Systems Fall Term | ENTR 110: Technology of Current & Future Energy Systems Course description: This course provides an overview of current and emerging technologies spanning the entire energy value chain—from generation to the grid edge. Students will explore a broad range of energy facilities and infrastructure, including traditional systems such as fossil fuels, nuclear power, and large-scale grids, while critically examining the ongoing transition to low-carbon and decentralized energy solutions. Topics include renewable energy integration (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal), smart grids, energy storage, electric vehicles, grid resilience, and next-generation clean energy technologies. Through real-world case studies, simulation exercises, and project-based learning, students will evaluate the trade-offs and system-level implications of various energy pathways. The course prepares students to make meaningful contributions to the development and deployment of resilient, efficient, and sustainable energy systems. Winter Term | ENTR 140: Data Analytics for Energy & Climate Course description: This course provides an introduction to the concepts and applications of data analytics for energy and climate. Topics include data collection and preparation, descriptive statistics, machine learning, optimization, and visualization. The course will introduce the overall process of using data analytics to solve problems, leveraging real-world data related to energy and climate. Students acquire a working knowledge of coding and analytics (Python or similar) with practical datasets related to electricity markets, power system operations, and climate. Spring Term | ENTR 170: Energy Systems Modeling Course description: This course introduces how to use and evaluate computational energy systems models to solve integrated technological, environmental, economic, cultural, and social problems. Foundational models of energy system operations, planning, investment, markets, technology adoption, and trade are introduced. Fundamental systems modeling topics are covered, including the treatment of uncertainty, spatial and temporal scaling, multi-sector dynamics, multi-stakeholder preferences, multiple objectives, and environmental and socioeconomic impacts (e.g., air quality, labor, land use, social equity). Existing, transforming, and emerging systems are explored, such as power, renewable, fossil fuel, hydrogen, carbon capture, transmission, industrial, residential, and transportation systems. Business and Economics of Energy Fall Term | ENTR 120: Team Dynamics & Professional Communications Course description: The evolving energy and climate workplace requires sophisticated professional skills. This course will serve as a laboratory for honing those skills in order to successfully pursue and perform in a meaningful career in the energy transition. Students will identify and apply core principles of teamwork, leadership, and communication, and will expand their ability to leverage skills in these areas to facilitate professional success. The course will include workshops and mentorship in career self-assessment, ethics, and interpersonal and organizational communication. Winter Term | ENTR 150: Energy Markets & Economics Course description: This course provides the conceptual and applied foundation in energy economics necessary to engage with the market frameworks at work in multiple sectors of the energy economy. Students will explore key aspects of energy supply and demand and assess the role of markets, regulation and deregulation in energy systems. The course addresses market design questions related to energy generation, transmission and distribution. It also provides an overview of economic institutions designed to control the impacts of energy infrastructure and examines market innovations that can advance energy policy goals and accelerate decarbonization. Spring Term | ENTR 180: Finance & Accounting for the Energy Transition Course description: The energy transition is a massive undertaking requiring trillions of dollars of investment. This course will explore concepts from finance and accounting that are crucial to understanding the rationale for investment decision-making.  We will work with various methods for assessing the financial viability of energy and decarbonization projects and managing financial risks. Critical topics that will be addressed include discounted cashflow modelling, financial & carbon accounting, investment risk analysis, & project financing. We will also explore ongoing innovations that seek to establish the next generation of financial products, services, and institutions that can effectively serve the goals of the energy transition. Students will develop both tactical and strategic skills to help them manage the financial aspects of energy projects, with the goal of becoming confident and conversant about the avenues available for securing commercial & concessional sources of funding. Science, Policy, and Impact of Energy Fall Term | ENTR 130: Climate Science & the Energy Transition Course description: This course will build on the basic principles of climate science to explore drivers of present-day climate change, including greenhouse gasses, and their impacts on society and ecosystems. With an emphasis on project-based learning, students will examine the interactions of climate change and economic growth, and how these affect a society's ability to navigate the energy transition. Critical to evaluate will be the socioecological costs and benefits of climate mitigation measures over short (years to decades) to long (decades to a century) time horizons, and at local to regional to global scales. Winter Term | ENTR 160: Energy Law & Policy Course description: This course will address the evolving U.S. policy context for energy system management and transition. We will briefly review historical approaches to managing energy resources before focusing on recent and emerging governance models as well as regulatory challenges and incentives for the deployment of emerging energy technologies. Throughout the course, we will examine the interplay between technological and social systems, including the key role of technology in both creating and mediating environmental impacts and the roles of policy and politics in shaping technology choices. We will use a diverse set of tools and methodologies to investigate the social and environmental implications of energy technology and policy choice. We will assess how these issues interact at multiple scales, particularly local, state, regional, and national, and review major global trends and their potential impact on U.S. energy law and policy. Spring Term | ENTR 190: Community & Global Resilience in Energy Transitions Course description: This course examines how energy systems and climate impacts reinforce longstanding social and economic inequities. Students will investigate who benefits and who is burdened, historically and today, across local and global contexts. Through a systems thinking lens, students will explore how natural and social systems are interconnected, interdependent, and shaped by dynamic feedback loops. Using this holistic approach, students will assess real-world case studies, identify leverage points for change, and analyze community-level climate and energy strategies from within and beyond the U.S. Emphasizing applied learning, students will engage in collaborative projects and comparative case analysis to develop actionable insights and equity-centered solutions. The course equips students with the systems literacy, effective engagement tools and techniques, and strategic frameworks needed for leadership in the energy transition and climate resilience field. Project-Based Courses Experiential learning is a cornerstone of the MET curriculum. Throughout the program, you'll encounter real-world scenarios in projects of varying scales. In some, you’ll partner with cross-sector organizations committed to decarbonization and sustainability. In all three thematic areas of the curriculum, you will wrestle with the complexity of transforming energy systems large and small—equipping you with skills and insights to directly implement in your career. Cross-sector Communication Skills Even as AI and technical advances transform the workforce, the skills that set professionals apart remain distinctly human: the capacity to work in teams, communicate across differences, and translate complex ideas into meaningful action. This is especially true in the energy sector, where every challenge sits at the intersection of multiple fields. Through our interdisciplinary curriculum, MET students gain fluency in speaking the languages of technology, finance, and policy. We go beyond concepts and theory, anchoring lessons in real-world projects and networking opportunities—because the best way to learn a new language is to speak it in practice. Alongside this fluency, you'll build core professional communication skills and develop your professional persona: practicing presentations, sharpening your interview technique, and learning what it takes to adapt your leadership and work styles in dynamic workplace environments. A Focus on Community Impact The MET program emphasizes equity and justice in how the energy transition affects social systems and communities, locally and globally. Because it's not just about the technology—decarbonization will only succeed if it's affordable, accessible, and fair, and if the people affected by it have a voice in shaping it. In the Community & Global Resilience in Energy Transitions (ENTR 190) course, MET students visit a local trail system to explore how regulation and land-use decisions shape energy systems and climate resilience on the ground. “The MET program reaffirmed that collaboration is key and people are key in the energy transition. Going into our careers, we will have to listen to all voices, loud and quiet, and incorporate those in a meaningful and respectful way to our solutions. People are the center of the energy issue and as long as we incorporate other people's perspectives in an equitable way, we will create energy outcomes that also promote societal good.” — Jordan Schisler, GR'26 Studying at the Irving Institute Situated between the Thayer School of Engineering and Tuck School of Business, with a direct view of the iconic Baker-Berry Library, the Institute serves as a hub of innovation, research, and collaboration. Our award-winning certified LEED Platinum facility was named 2024 Building of the Year by the New Hampshire Chapter of the U.S. Green Building Council (USGBC). The building was also awarded the prestigious American Institute of Architects (AIA) Committee on the Environment (COTE) 2025 Top Ten Award, recognizing sustainable design excellence. Inside, you'll find flexible classrooms, collaborative project spaces, and the inviting Fern Coffee and Tea Bar, ideal for a break between classes. MET students also have exclusive access to the Sandra L. Irving 1972a Commons, a full kitchen where they can store and prepare meals and drinks. Downstairs, a dedicated MET Lounge offers students their own space to relax and recharge. “Throughout the program, I worked on projects exploring affordable housing decarbonization, energy resilience in rural coastal communities across Maine, battery energy storage deployment, grid modernization, energy systems modeling, climate and energy data analytics, and campus decarbonization strategies. These experiences strengthened my understanding of how energy systems, policy, infrastructure, economics, and communities intersect, and reinforced my passion for developing solutions that are both technically effective and socially equitable.” Rebecca Middlen GR'26 Learning Outcomes Upon completing the program, you'll be prepared to collaborate with a wide range of stakeholders across the technical, economic, political, and social dimensions of energy systems and transitions. The MET program equips you with the skills, knowledge, and network to succeed in a rapidly evolving energy landscape. Program-Level Competencies Describe and analyze major dimensions of energy systems and transitions, including technological, business and financial, policy, and social dimensions. Develop and apply analytical frameworks and problem-solving skills to creatively address specific and systemic energy transition challenges. Contribute to, build, and lead multidisciplinary teams and partner effectively with diverse stakeholders. Assess the distribution of benefits and burdens in specific energy system contexts and propose actions that accelerate an affordable, reliable, equitable clean energy transition for all. Build skills necessary to thrive in current and future careers in the rapidly changing energy & climate industry. Connect with Us Ready to learn more? We do not accept paper application materials. Official transcripts should not be sent to the Guarini School office during the application process. Application Fee $150 GRE Not accepted. English Language Proficiency Non-U.S. citizens are required to submit language proficiency test scores, with the exception of those who have earned, or are currently earning, an undergraduate (bachelor's degree or equivalent) or higher degree after having studied for at least four years at an institution in the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, Australia, Ireland, or New Zealand where English was the sole primary language of instruction. We accept TOEFL, IELTS, and Duolingo The ETS code for the Guarini School is 3351 Personal Statements The MET provides an intensive, multidisciplinary, small-cohort experience.  Please write a brief essay explaining how the MET will equip you to achieve your goals as a future energy/climate professional. Use the following prompts as a guide to answering this question in no more than 1000 words. What is distinctive about the MET that will contribute to your career aspirations? What personal educational/professional areas of growth do you believe the MET may help you address and contribute to your work in accelerating the energy transition? Reflect on an educational or professional experience. How has it contributed to the early stages of your development or aspirations for working in the climate and energy space? Recommendation Letters 3 required, up to 4 accepted. If you are within 5 years of completing your undergraduate degree, we would expect at least two references to come from undergraduate instructors. References should speak to your ability to handle a rigorous academic workload and should reflect substantial academic, professional, and/or civic (e.g. volunteering) responsibilities or work. Resume/ CV Transcripts Your most recent unofficial transcripts should be uploaded as part of your application. Official transcripts are not needed during the application process. Financial Aid When you fill out your graduate program application, please indicate if you are considering applying for financial aid. Applying for aid will not affect your admissions process or commit you to anything, but it's important for us to know as soon as possible if you might be interested in financial aid. If you are, be sure to fill out the CSS Profile (CSS Code: 3357). Indicate your year in college as "1st-year grad/prof." CSS should be submitted at the same time as your graduate application. Enrollment Deposit A non-refundable $500 enrollment deposit is required upon acceptance of an admission offer. QUESTIONS ABOUT THE ADMISSIONS PROCESS Admissions information can be found here. No additional application is required to be considered. Your admissions application will be reviewed upon submission for a merit scholarship. Learn more about MET scholarships . Learn more about financial aid for graduate students . Can international students apply for financial aid? Yes. International students can apply for a need-based Master of Energy Transition (MET) scholarship . There are options for additional financial support for international students as well. For example, there are student employment opportunities , and international students may be eligible for certain private loans . You can contact the Dartmouth Financial Aid office for more information about loans for international students. Courses & Curriculum Who are the instructors? A talented group of Dartmouth professors, lecturers, and expert practitioner-instructors teach our courses, ensuring you are immersed in a broad range of academic and professional perspectives and expertise. Meet the MET faculty . Do Master of Energy Transition (MET) students conduct research? The MET is a professional degree program and emphasizes real-world experience through project-based courses. There are no formal research or thesis components or requirements. Is there an internship requirement? The Master of Energy Transition program does not require a formal internship. Instead, experiential learning is interwoven throughout the curriculum . Our project-based courses serve as mini-internships — allowing you to gain hands-on experience with real-world challenges through our partner organizations. This is one of many opportunities to build your skills and professional network. If you are seeking a formal internship outside of the program, you'll find that the schedule of the program allows for a summer internship prior to the program start or following graduation. Careers & Mentorship What are the mentorship and industry experience opportunities? Expert mentorship and real-world experience are built into the core of the Master of Energy Transition program. Mentorship: When you begin the program, you'll be thoughtfully paired with a mentor from our vast community of Dartmouth alumni energy and climate leaders. Mentors will provide support throughout the program, including personalized career advice and networking opportunities. Projects: You'll complete several project-based courses, enabling you to gain real-world experience. Through our partnerships with leading industries and organizations, we offer highly relevant and timely hands-on projects and data sets. Master of Energy Transition Faculty Director, Professor Geoff Parker , holds more than a decade of experience building and teaching highly impactful industry-engaged project courses. What career resources and support are available for Master of Energy Transition students? You’ll benefit from personalized career mentorship and support, along with opportunities for professional development, including career treks where you’ll meet industry leaders as well as career panels featuring a diverse range of professionals. Our dedicated program staff, faculty, and engaged alumni network offer timely insight into the skills and experience that today’s employers value across business, non-profit, and government sectors. Additionally, GuariniGRAD offers Career Development resources and guidance . What types of jobs are graduates prepared for? The Master of Energy Transition equips students with multidisciplinary knowledge and skills essential for a wide range of positions in energy, climate, sustainability, and adjacent fields. Potential roles include: Energy and/or climate analyst Consulting and coordinating roles in business, policy, and sustainability Project and program management and leadership roles for corporate, government, and non-profit entities Communications and engagement positions View more energy sector career information . Student Life Where can I learn more about being a graduate student at Dartmouth? Dartmouth offers comprehensive graduate student support in academics, career development, community, professional development, and wellness. Visit the GuariniGRAD site to learn more . Explore the MET Courses & Curriculum View course info View course info MET Faculty Meet our faculty Meet our faculty Mentorship & Community Learn about our community Learn about our community Connect with Us Ready to learn more? Sign up to receive program information and join us for an upcoming Info Session. Request more info Request more info Attend an Info Session Attend an Info Session Have questions? Talk with our knowledgeable admissions manager about your goals, and get answers to your questions about MET courses, faculty, mentorship, and how to apply. Madeleine Bothe, MET Recruitment and Admissions Manager Two easy ways to connect: Send an email : energy.transition@dartmouth.edu Schedule an online conversation Join our Next Info Session After you attend an Info Session, your MET application fee will be waived! Join our faculty director, program director, and members of the MET team to hear about courses and faculty, personalized mentorship, and career treks. title: Drilling of Geothermal Test Wells to Begin Next Week | Campus Services
text: Articles Drilling of Geothermal Test Wells to Begin Next Week The work is part of Dartmouth's transition to a noncombustion energy future. Image A geothermal test well is drilled on the Green in 2019. (Photo By Chris Johnson) 9/20/2022 More Reading https://home.dartmouth.edu/news/2022/03/dartmouth-heating-system-upgrades-draw-… Dartmouth will drill test wells in four locations beginning next week to test each site's viability as a future geothermal well field. The work is part of Dartmouth's transition toward a noncombustion energy future, which includes eliminating the use of fuel oil to heat the campus' almost 130 buildings. The four well locations are: between the Maynard parking lot and Kellogg Hall; northeast of Scully-Fahey Field; between Burnham Field and the Thompson parking lot; and in the northwest corner of the Dewey parking lot. Drilling on the Maynard site is scheduled to begin on Sept. 27 at 8 a.m. and run through 5 p.m. each day for approximately three days. The Scully-Fahey site will be the second drilling location, followed by the Thompson site, and then the Dewey lot location. In total, the drilling is expected to take a total of two to three weeks and will not be done on weekends. Quote Our geothermal investigation is an important part of our larger transition to renewable energy systems, which is going to shape the future of Dartmouth for the next 100 years in terms of how we are going to heat and cool our buildings. Attribution Julia Pfeiffer, program manager for energy infrastructure renewal Community members are invited to stop by the Maynard site on Sept. 27 from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. to talk with Dartmouth staff about the project. "Our geothermal investigation is an important part of our larger transition to renewable energy systems, which is going to shape the future of Dartmouth for the next 100 years in terms of how we are going to heat and cool our buildings," says Julia Pfeiffer , program manager for Dartmouth's energy infrastructure renewal. Dartmouth currently uses a geothermal system to heat and cool the Fahey and McLane residence halls, with 13 wells that were installed near the building in 2007. The systems can be built under buildings or on open land. Once installed, they are below ground and the land on top of them can be used for other purposes—as home to buildings, playing fields, and parking lots. Geothermal systems, also called geoexchange systems, are among the thermal energy system technologies that Dartmouth is investigating. Other energy projects include improving energy efficiency by upgrading aging buildings and infrastructure, exploring large-scale solar projects, and continuing the transition from steam heating to more efficient hot-water heating. The energy transition is the foundation of Dartmouth's plan to significantly reduce greenhouse gas emissions , which as of 2020 have declined 27% from 2010 levels. The institutional goal is a 50% reduction by 2025. The geothermal drilling will look like drilling for a typical residential water well and also resemble the geothermal test well Dartmouth dug on the Green in 2019. The results of that test well showed that the land under the Green could work for ground source heating and cooling. Installation of geothermal well fields—which could each have hundreds of wells, about 6 inches in diameter, and from 200 to 800 feet deep—is likely six months to a year off, says Pfeiffer. After the holes are drilled, there will be a series of tests done to investigate properties such as flow, temperature, and geology. Geoexchange systems, which extract thermal energy from the ground, are typically paired with heat pumps that provide heating or cooling for temperature control in buildings. Heat pumps use electricity to provide heating or cooling and can be entirely noncombustion if the electricity is derived from renewable sources such as solar, wind, and hydroelectric technologies. The technology is practical and sensible, recalling the use of root cellars to draw cooling and warmth from the ground, says Rosi Kerr , director of sustainability. "This process is both innovative and, in its simplicity, a return to our roots," she says. Written by Office of Communications Share this
